records.applicability_limits: Defines a container, not the taxonomy; the type URIs and their stability are still the API owner's design work. Adds a second media type to negotiate, which is friction for tiny internal APIs.
records.counter_evidence: Microsoft Azure guidelines mandate a different, incompatible error envelope (error.code / error.message plus x-ms-error-code header) rather than problem+json, showing large estates diverge from the RFC.

records.source: RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures
records.licence: IETF Trust Legal Provisions (BSD-style, RFC text)
records.finding: A signature is only as good as its base string: canonicalise an explicit, ordered list of covered components (fields plus derived values such as method, path, authority) so signer and verifier build byte-identical input despite lawful intermediary rewriting, and bind created, expires and nonce for replay control.
records.applicability_limits: Covers request and response signing generally, not webhook delivery specifically; requires a canonicalisation library on both sides and is heavier than a single HMAC-over-raw-body scheme. Adoption outside standards-conscious estates is still thin.
records.counter_evidence: Standard Webhooks and GitHub both ship simpler HMAC-over-a-fixed-string schemes rather than RFC 9421, and dominate real webhook traffic.

records.source: RFC 9745 The Deprecation HTTP Response Header Field
records.licence: IETF Trust Legal Provisions (BSD-style, RFC text)
records.finding: Deprecation is announced in-band and dated, and removal is a separate later date: Deprecation carries when the resource became or becomes deprecated, RFC 8594 Sunset carries when it stops responding, and Sunset must not be earlier than Deprecation.
records.applicability_limits: Informational only, it changes no behaviour, so it works solely if consumers instrument for it. Says nothing about how long the gap between the two dates should be.

records.source: Standard Webhooks specification
records.version_or_commit: spec version 1.0.0, main branch as at 2026-08-03
records.finding: Sign the triple id.timestamp.payload, not the payload alone: the id gives the consumer a natural idempotency key, the timestamp gives a replay window, and the versioned signature prefix (v1 HMAC-SHA256, v1a ed25519) plus multi-signature headers give zero-downtime key rotation. Constant-time comparison and signing exactly the bytes transmitted are mandatory.
records.applicability_limits: Does not fix a numeric timestamp tolerance, so each estate must pick one. Payload guidance (type, timestamp, data; under about 20kb) is a convention, not enforceable. Vendor-originated (Svix) despite the neutral name.
records.counter_evidence: GitHub, Stripe and Slack each ship incompatible bespoke schemes; there is no convergence in practice, so a consumer library must still special-case per provider.

records.source: GitHub webhook delivery validation documentation
records.finding: Verify against the raw request body before any parsing or re-encoding, and compare digests in constant time; a framework that hands you a parsed object has already destroyed the bytes the signature covers.
records.applicability_limits: One vendor's scheme, with no timestamp header and therefore no built-in replay window; the raw-body and constant-time lessons generalise, the header layout does not.
records.licence_evidence: Footer reads "© 2026 GitHub, Inc." followed by links to Terms and Privacy. Raw HTML fetched at 200/165KB contains zero occurrences of the string "licence"/"license". No CC licence is stated on the page despite the github/docs repo carrying one.

records.source: draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header (IETF HTTPAPI WG)
records.version_or_commit: draft-07, intended status Standards Track, expiry 2026-04-18; no RFC number as at 2026-08-03
records.finding: A client-generated Idempotency-Key request header makes POST and PATCH fault-tolerant, moving retry safety from server-side guesswork to an explicit contract term the client controls.
records.applicability_limits: Still an expired-window Internet-Draft after several years, so the header name is de facto rather than de jure; do not cite it as a ratified standard. Says nothing binding about retention windows or conflict semantics.
records.counter_evidence: Microsoft Azure guidelines instead mandate OASIS Repeatable Requests headers (Repeatability-Request-ID, Repeatability-First-Sent), so the header name is genuinely contested at scale.

records.source: draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers (IETF HTTPAPI WG)
records.version_or_commit: draft-11 dated 2026-05-23, intended status Standards Track, expiry 2026-11-24; no RFC number as at 2026-08-03
records.finding: Split the static quota policy (RateLimit-Policy) from the live remaining budget (RateLimit) so a client can plan its call pattern in advance rather than discovering limits only by being refused.
records.applicability_limits: Draft, not an RFC, and the field syntax has churned across eleven revisions; pinning to a specific draft number is required for interoperability. Advisory only, it does not define enforcement or 429 behaviour.

records.source: Google AIP-180 Backwards compatibility
records.finding: Compatibility is three separate guarantees that must each hold: source, wire and semantic. Renaming is removal plus addition and therefore breaking; so are moving a field into or out of a oneof, changing a type, changing a default, changing a resource-name format, and adding a required request field.
records.applicability_limits: Written for protobuf-shaped APIs at Google scale; the semantic-compatibility bar (no change to how a value is constructed) is stricter than most estates can afford. Enum additions are flagged as risky rather than forbidden, which leaves a judgement call.

records.source: Google AIP-158 Pagination
records.finding: Page tokens must be opaque and non-parseable, must bind to the filter and ordering of the call that issued them (mismatched follow-up parameters are an INVALID_ARGUMENT error), must never carry authorisation, and total counts are optional and may be an estimate.
records.applicability_limits: Opacity forbids the client-side tricks (jump to page N, resume from an arbitrary offset) that some consumers expect; suits list-and-stream consumption, not table UIs that need page numbers.
records.counter_evidence: JSON:API reserves a page parameter family but deliberately stays strategy-agnostic, so offset paging remains conformant there.

records.source: Zalando RESTful API Guidelines
records.version_or_commit: web edition as served 2026-08-03, targeting OpenAPI 3.1
records.finding: A working corporate rulebook is a graded one: MUST for API-first definition in OpenAPI before code, no URL versioning, media-type versioning, no backward-incompatible change and problem+json errors; SHOULD for cursor pagination and idempotent POST/PATCH via an Idempotency-Key. The MUST list is short enough to be enforceable.
records.applicability_limits: Media-type versioning is a minority position and is poorly supported by browsers, caches and casual clients; adopting it wholesale imports tooling pain. Written for a large multi-team retailer, so the review ceremony does not fit a small estate.
records.counter_evidence: Microsoft Azure guidelines mandate an api-version query parameter, directly contradicting both URL and media-type positions, and are equally battle-tested.

records.source: Microsoft Azure REST API Guidelines
records.licence: unknown (repository licence file not inspected; repo commonly Apache-2.0 or CC-BY-4.0)
records.finding: Make the version explicit and mandatory rather than defaulted: a required api-version query parameter using YYYY-MM-DD with a -preview suffix, a 400 with a named error code when it is missing or unknown, error codes treated as contract (a new top-level code needs a version bump), and slow calls promoted to long-running operations with a 202 plus operation-location status monitor retained at least 24 hours.
records.applicability_limits: Mandatory-version-parameter and LRO machinery presume a large managed-service estate with generated SDKs; both are heavy for an internal API with two consumers. Rejecting a call for a missing api-version is hostile to exploratory clients.
records.counter_evidence: Zalando forbids URL versioning and mandates media-type versioning; Stripe (EV-0061) uses an account-pinned date header. Three mature estates, three incompatible answers.

records.source: Stripe idempotent requests documentation
records.finding: Idempotency needs four decided parameters, not one header: the stored result is the status code and body of the first attempt including 5xx; retention is at least 24 hours after which the same key starts a fresh request; replaying a key with different parameters is an error, not a silent overwrite; and a request conflicting with a concurrently executing one is not cached and is safe to retry.
records.applicability_limits: Applies to POST only, since GET and DELETE are idempotent by definition. Caching a 500 means a client that retries a genuinely transient failure with the same key gets the failure back forever, which pushes retry-with-new-key policy onto the client.
records.licence_evidence: Raw HTML fetched at 200/1.24MB contains zero occurrences of the string "licence"/"license". The rendered page is API reference prose only, with no rights, licence or terms statement.

records.source: JSON:API specification
records.finding: A media type can evolve without a version negotiation mechanism at all if it commits publicly to never remove, only add; JSON:API makes that the governing rule and keeps its version field optional as a result.
records.applicability_limits: Never-remove is affordable for a wire format with no business semantics; a product API accumulating dead fields forever pays a real comprehension and maintenance cost. The document conventions (type/id/relationships/included) are opinionated and unsuited to non-resource-shaped domains.
records.counter_evidence: Stripe (EV-0061) demonstrates the opposite bet: roughly a hundred deliberate incompatible changes survived only because version transformation modules were built to absorb them.

records.source: Buf breaking-change rule categories
records.finding: Compatibility is not binary but a chosen strictness tier, and the tier should be declared: FILE (default, protects generated code layout), PACKAGE, WIRE_JSON (minimum where JSON transports are used), WIRE (binary only). Start strict and relax deliberately rather than discovering the tier by breaking someone.
records.applicability_limits: Protobuf-specific; the tier vocabulary does not map cleanly onto JSON-over-HTTP, where there is no equivalent of generated-file placement. Requires a stored baseline to diff against.
records.licence_evidence: Footer reads "© 2026 Buf Technologies, Inc." with links to Terms of Use and Privacy Policy, but names no licence for the documentation. The only "License" strings in the HTML are Font Awesome attribution comments ("Icons: CC BY 4.0, Fonts: SIL OFL 1.1, Code: MIT License, Copyright 2025 Fonticons, Inc."), which licence the icon set, not the page content.

records.source: oasdiff (OpenAPI diff and breaking-change detector)
records.version_or_commit: main branch, 1,892 commits, approx 1.3k stars, as at 2026-08-03
records.finding: Breaking-change detection can be mechanised against the spec itself: a breaking command gates the build, a separate changelog command reports consumer-visible but non-breaking changes, and the classification rules are configurable rather than hard-coded, so an estate can encode its own compatibility promise.
records.applicability_limits: Detects only what the spec expresses; semantic breaks that leave the schema unchanged (a field's meaning or units altered) pass silently. Requires a committed baseline spec and therefore only works where the spec is generated or authored reliably.

records.source: Spectral JSON/YAML API style-guide linter
records.version_or_commit: develop branch, 2,239 commits, approx 3.2k stars, as at 2026-08-03; supports OpenAPI 2/3.0/3.1, AsyncAPI 2.x, Arazzo 1.0
records.finding: API conventions only bind if they are executable: a ruleset turns house style (naming, required descriptions, error shapes, forbidden patterns) into a lint run that fails, which is the difference between a guideline document and governance.
records.applicability_limits: No OpenAPI 3.2 support listed as at the access date, which matters if the pack standardises on 3.2. Linting checks form, never behaviour, so a lint-clean spec can still describe a service that does something else.

records.source: CloudEvents specification (CNCF)
records.version_or_commit: v1.0.2 latest release; 1,124 commits on main; CNCF graduated 2024-01-25
records.finding: Standardise the event envelope (id, source, type, specversion, time) separately from the payload, so routing, deduplication and tracing work across transports without every consumer relearning a bespoke metadata layout.
records.applicability_limits: Governs metadata only; payload schema and its evolution remain entirely the producer's problem, which is where most event breakage actually happens. Version has sat at 1.0.2 for a long stretch, so treat it as stable rather than evolving.

records.source: Confluent Schema Registry schema evolution and compatibility
records.finding: For event contracts the compatibility mode encodes an upgrade order and must be chosen before the first schema change: BACKWARD (default, consumers first), FORWARD (producers first), FULL (either order, add or remove optional fields only), NONE (lockstep). Transitive variants check every prior version, not just the last, which is the only mode safe for replayable logs.
records.applicability_limits: Vendor documentation for one registry; the mode names are Confluent's, though the underlying upgrade-order logic is general. Non-transitive modes give a false sense of safety when consumers rewind a topic to its start.
records.licence_evidence: Footer reads "Copyright © Confluent, Inc. 2014-" plus trademark notice for Apache marks, and links to Terms & Conditions and Privacy Policy. No content licence is named. The "License" links present in the side navigation point to installation/license.html and connect/license.html, which concern Confluent product licence keys, not documentation reuse.

records.source: GraphQL specification, September 2025 edition
records.version_or_commit: September2025 edition current release; prerelease working draft dated 2026-04-02
records.licence: unknown (spec text served under an Open Web Foundation agreement; licence page not retrieved)
records.finding: GraphQL replaces API versioning with continuous schema evolution: fields are added freely and retired via deprecation because a client only receives what it explicitly selected, so additions cannot break existing queries.
records.applicability_limits: The spec text itself returned HTTP 403 to automated retrieval at the access date, so the edition and date come from the publisher's version index rather than the document. The no-versioning claim holds for field additions and holds much less for type, nullability or argument changes.
records.counter_evidence: Never removing fields means schemas accrete indefinitely; deprecation without a sunset date is not removal, so the version problem is deferred rather than solved.

records.source: Brito and Valente, REST vs GraphQL: A Controlled Experiment
records.study_design: Within-subjects controlled experiment; 22 participants (10 undergraduate, 12 graduate) each implemented eight queries against a web service using both GraphQL and REST
records.population: 22 university students, ICSA 2020
records.finding: GraphQL reduced client query implementation effort against REST (median 6 minutes versus 9), and the gap widened for REST endpoints with several parameters; the benefit held for participants with REST but no GraphQL experience.
records.applicability_limits: Students, not professionals; measures first-write time for eight queries only, and says nothing about server implementation cost, operational cost, caching, authorisation or long-term maintenance, which is where GraphQL's real bill arrives.
records.counter_evidence: The single measured dimension (client authoring time) is the dimension GraphQL is designed to optimise; the experiment does not measure the server-side and security costs that drive most GraphQL regret.

records.source: Zetterlund, Tiwari, Monperrus and Baudry, Harvesting Production GraphQL Queries to Detect Schema Faults
records.study_design: Tool construction (AutoGraphQL) plus empirical evaluation against two production GraphQL applications
records.population: Two production GraphQL APIs (Saleor e-commerce, Frontapp)
records.finding: Tests derived from real production queries covered 26.9 percent of the Saleor schema and 48.7 percent of the Frontapp schema and found eight schema faults, exercising parts of the API the developers' own suites never touched.
records.applicability_limits: Two applications only, and GraphQL-specific. The low coverage figures are the point: a permissive schema surface far exceeds what any consumer actually exercises, so most of a large GraphQL schema is effectively untested attack surface.

records.source: Hatfield-Dodds and Dygalo, Deriving Semantics-Aware Fuzzers from Web API Schemas (Schemathesis)
records.study_design: Comparative evaluation of schema-derived fuzzers against 16 real-world web services
records.population: 16 open-source and production web services with OpenAPI or GraphQL schemas
records.finding: A machine-readable schema is not only documentation but an executable test oracle: schema-derived property-based fuzzing found 1.4 to 4.5 times more unique defects than the next-best fuzzer per target, and was the only tool to find defects in four of sixteen services.
records.applicability_limits: Preprint rather than a peer-reviewed venue record; 16 services is a small sample and the authors evaluate their own tool. Findings depend on schema fidelity, so an inaccurate or generated-after-the-fact spec yields weak fuzzing.

records.source: Wittern, Cha and Laredo, Generating GraphQL-Wrappers for REST(-like) APIs
records.study_design: Tool construction (OASGraph) plus large-scale evaluation over publicly available OpenAPI documents
records.population: 959 publicly available OpenAPI Specification documents
records.finding: Automated transformation from a REST contract to a GraphQL schema succeeded for 89.5 percent of 959 real specifications but with limitations in many cases, the failures traced to missing or ambiguous information in the specifications themselves. Downstream automation is capped by contract quality, not by tooling.
records.applicability_limits: 2018 corpus of OpenAPI 2/3.0 documents; specification quality and tooling have both moved since, so the exact percentage is stale. The principle that under-specified contracts defeat generation is the durable part.

records.source: TypeSpec API definition language (Microsoft)
records.version_or_commit: main branch, 5,929 commits, approx 5.8k stars, as at 2026-08-03
records.finding: When contract-first is adopted, author the contract in a language with reuse and linting rather than hand-writing OpenAPI: package house patterns as libraries so the conforming choice is the easy one, and emit OpenAPI, clients and docs from the single definition.
records.applicability_limits: Adds a compile step and a second language to learn between intent and the emitted spec; the emitted OpenAPI is a build artefact, which complicates any workflow that expects to hand-edit it. Vendor-led despite the MIT licence, with roadmap set by Azure needs.
records.counter_evidence: OpenAPI itself (EV-0023) deliberately declines to prescribe design-first over code-first, and code-first generation from annotated handlers keeps spec and implementation from drifting apart by construction.

records.source: ArchUnit
records.licence: Apache-2.0 (bundles ASM under BSD and Guava under Apache-2.0)
records.finding: Architecture rules can be expressed as ordinary unit tests over compiled bytecode, so layering, slice independence and cycle bans fail the normal build rather than a separate audit tool. A boundary rule that runs in the test suite is the cheapest form of enforcement because it needs no new CI surface.
records.applicability_limits: JVM bytecode only. Cannot see dynamic dispatch through reflection, string-keyed service locators or configuration-driven wiring, so rules can pass while a runtime boundary is still crossed. Says nothing about which boundaries are correct.
records.counter_evidence: Bytecode-level rules bind to package names, so a rename can silently disable a rule unless the rule set itself is reviewed; frozen-violation baselines let debt accumulate invisibly.
records.review: on-change-of:ArchUnit major version or Java module system adoption

records.source: import-linter
records.finding: Boundary enforcement in a dynamic language works at the import graph, with three named contract shapes that cover most real rules: layers (ordered, higher may import lower), forbidden (this must never reach that) and independence (these siblings must not know each other). Declaring the contract in a config file makes the intended architecture a reviewable artefact rather than folklore.
records.applicability_limits: Python only, and static imports only. Runtime imports, plugin registries, dependency-injection containers and string-based dynamic loading are invisible to it. Contract file must be kept in step with package renames by hand.
records.counter_evidence: Import-graph rules cannot express allowed direction of data flow or call semantics, so a module can import only what it should and still be tightly coupled through a shared mutable object.
records.review: on-change-of:import-linter contract types or Python import machinery

records.source: dependency-cruiser
records.finding: The same rule engine that fails a build on a boundary violation can emit the dependency graph as dot, mermaid, json or html, so the enforced architecture and the drawn architecture come from one source. Rule classes worth having by default are: no cycles, no orphans, no production code importing dev or optional dependencies, no reaching into another module's internals.
records.applicability_limits: JavaScript, TypeScript and CoffeeScript module graphs. Detects structural violations only; does not evaluate whether the module decomposition is sound. Large monorepos need explicit include and exclude tuning or run time becomes a problem.
records.counter_evidence: Generated graphs of a large codebase are usually unreadable, so the visualisation claim only pays off when scoped to a folder or a rule violation.

records.source: arc42 architecture documentation template
records.version_or_commit: unknown (web overview inspected 2026-08-03; template in use since 2005)
records.licence: unknown (site states open source and free including commercial use; specific licence page not inspected)
records.finding: A durable architecture description answers twelve fixed questions, of which only three are diagrams (building block, runtime, deployment). The other nine carry goals, constraints, scope, solution strategy, crosscutting concepts, decisions, quality requirements, risks and glossary. The decision-relevant lesson is that diagrams are a minority of an architecture record; a pack that ships only diagram guidance leaves most of the record unspecified.
records.applicability_limits: A template, not a method: it says where content goes, never how to derive it or whether it is right. Full twelve-section documents are heavy for a single-service venture and go stale unless generated or gated.
records.counter_evidence: Section-complete templates invite box-filling; the arc42 canvas exists precisely because the full template is too much for many systems.

records.source: Alistair Cockburn, Hexagonal Architecture (Ports and Adapters)
records.licence: unknown (author's site, no explicit licence found)
records.finding: The stated goal is testability and symmetry, not layering: the application must be drivable equally by a user, another program, an automated test or a batch script, and must be developable in isolation from its eventual runtime devices. The decision rule that follows is that a port earns its existence when a second driver or a second device is genuinely plausible; otherwise the adapter is ceremony.
records.applicability_limits: A 2005 pattern statement with no empirical evaluation, written before managed cloud services and typed generated clients. Says nothing about deployment topology or data ownership.
records.counter_evidence: Applied uniformly it produces an adapter per dependency and a mapping layer per boundary, which for a small venture costs more than the substitution it buys; the original text does not bound the pattern's scope.

records.source: DORA capability: loosely coupled teams and architecture
records.study_design: Capability page summarising DORA's multi-year cross-sectional survey programme with structural equation modelling; this page reports predictive claims, not the underlying model output
records.population: Self-selected survey respondents across industries and company sizes, tens of thousands of professionals across programme years
records.finding: Architectural coupling is measured by observable outcomes, not by style label: proportion of changes needing approval outside the team, ability to deploy independently, ability to test in isolation without an integrated environment, contract test failure rate, and frequency of unplanned work caused by upstream change. DORA is explicit that the label does not determine the outcome, since organisations fail with microservices and succeed with mainframes.
records.applicability_limits: Self-reported cross-sectional survey data from mostly team-scale and enterprise-scale organisations; predictive language is correlational, and this page gives no effect sizes. Very little of the population resembles a one-to-three person venture.
records.counter_evidence: The same programme's framing is often quoted as an argument for service splitting, which the page itself contradicts by locating the capability in independent deployability and testability rather than in process count.

records.source: Ghemawat, Grandl, Petrovic, Whittaker, Towards Modern Development of Cloud Applications (HotOS '23)
records.study_design: Workshop position paper with a prototype framework and benchmark comparison against a microservice deployment of the same application
records.population: Google-authored prototype (Service Weaver) and its own example applications
records.benchmark: Latency and cloud cost of one application deployed as microservices versus as co-located components
records.licence: unknown (ACM proceedings; author PDF hosted by SIGOPS)
records.finding: The core defect named is conflating logical boundaries with physical boundaries: microservice frameworks force the module decomposition and the process decomposition to be the same decision, taken early and expensively. Separating them lets a single logical decomposition be deployed as one process or many. Reported gains for co-located deployment of the same modules were up to 15x latency and up to 9x cost.
records.applicability_limits: A position paper, not a field study; the numbers come from the authors' own prototype and example workloads in Go, with no independent replication and no long-lived production evidence. Assumes a single organisation controls all components.
records.counter_evidence: Independent follow-up analysis of Service Weaver (arXiv 2404.09357) treats it as a promising direction rather than a settled result; the framework's own maturity has since been questioned, so the principle is transferable but the tool is not.
records.review: on-change-of:independent replication of the co-location cost claim

records.source: Martin Fowler, MonolithFirst
records.finding: Service boundaries are discovered rather than designed, so paying the distribution premium before the boundaries are known buys the wrong boundaries at the highest price. The stated decision rule is to start in one deployable and split when a boundary has proved itself stable under change.
records.applicability_limits: Explicitly anecdotal. The author states he lacks enough cases to decide when the strategy applies and that any advice on the question is tentative. Eleven years old and predates managed serverless defaults.
records.counter_evidence: The same author hosts the counter-argument that a team with prior domain experience can and should start with services; the position is contested even within its own source.

records.source: MacCormack, Baldwin and Rusnak, Exploring the duality between product and organizational architectures (Research Policy 41(8), 2012)
records.study_design: Natural experiment comparing dependency structure of paired products of equivalent function built by tightly coupled commercial firms versus loosely coupled open source communities, using design structure matrices
records.population: Matched pairs of substantial software products (commercial and open source)
records.benchmark: Propagation cost and modularity measures derived from call and dependency graphs
records.licence: unknown (publisher copyright; open-access author copy via Harvard DASH)
records.finding: Product structure mirrors the communication structure of the organisation that built it, and the effect held across matched pairs of functionally equivalent systems. The operational consequence is that an architecture rule fights the org chart it contradicts, so for a solo or two-person venture the mirroring prediction is a single tightly coupled artefact unless boundaries are enforced mechanically.
records.applicability_limits: Studies large multi-person organisations and open source communities; nothing in the sample resembles a one-person team or an agent-run codebase. Correlational within a natural experiment, and design structure matrices measure static dependency only.
records.counter_evidence: Later work on the mirroring hypothesis finds partial mirroring and deliberate 'mirror breaking' by firms that invest in interface standards, so mirroring is a default tendency rather than a law.

records.source: SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH specification, Reproducible Builds
records.finding: Determinism is achievable by naming the specific non-determinism and clamping it. The normative rules are narrow and testable: the value must be an integer epoch reproducible from source alone, builds must use it instead of the current time, embedded non-current timestamps must be clamped to no later than it, the variable must not be unset for child processes, and locale or timezone formatting must be deferred to runtime. Verification is byte comparison of two independent builds, not inspection.
records.applicability_limits: Timestamps only. Does not address build path, locale, filesystem ordering, parallelism-dependent output, embedded random seeds, network-fetched dependencies or non-deterministic compilers. A build honouring the whole specification can still fail to reproduce.
records.counter_evidence: Ongoing issue classes recorded by the project (for example timezone-dependent behaviour in specific compilers, January 2026 report) show the variable is necessary and far from sufficient.

records.source: Bazel documentation, Hermeticity
records.version_or_commit: docs for Bazel 8.6 line, page last updated 2026-07-14
records.finding: Hermeticity is defined as same source plus same configuration yielding the same output by isolating the build from the host, and it is bought with two concrete moves: treat tools as versioned source dependencies rather than host installations, and identify inputs by content hash. The payoff claimed is not purity but cacheability, safe parallelism, several toolchain versions coexisting, and reproducible debugging.
records.applicability_limits: Vendor documentation for a build system whose adoption cost is high; the guidance assumes a monorepo and a team able to maintain toolchain definitions. No measured effect sizes given.
records.counter_evidence: Full hermeticity conflicts with fetching dependencies from live package registries, which most small ventures do; partial hermeticity via lockfiles plus a pinned container image is the cheaper point on the curve and this page does not price it.

records.source: Chris Richardson, Transactional Outbox pattern (microservices.io)
records.licence: unknown (site copyright, no open licence stated)
records.finding: Whenever a state change and an outbound message must both happen, writing the message into the same database transaction and relaying it separately removes the need for two-phase commit and guarantees the message is sent if and only if the transaction committed. The accepted cost is at-least-once delivery, so every consumer must be idempotent by construction.
records.applicability_limits: Assumes a transactional database and a relay process (log tailing or polling). Does not solve ordering across aggregates, and adds a moving part that must be monitored. Irrelevant where there is no message broker.
records.counter_evidence: The pattern relies on developers remembering to write to the outbox rather than publishing directly, which is exactly the discipline a boundary rule should enforce mechanically; the source offers no enforcement mechanism.

records.source: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2022, Software, systems and enterprise: Architecture description
records.version_or_commit: second edition, published 2022-11-07, cancels and replaces ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2011
records.licence: proprietary (ISO copyright, paid access; catalogue page and public abstract only were read)
records.finding: The standard normalises the vocabulary an architecture record needs: stakeholders and their concerns, viewpoints that frame those concerns, views that conform to viewpoints, model kinds, and correspondence rules between views. The transferable rule is that a view exists to answer a named concern of a named stakeholder, so any diagram with no stated concern is undefended and can be cut.
records.applicability_limits: Paywalled, so only the catalogue abstract was inspected; conformance is aimed at enterprise and systems-of-systems documentation, and the standard prescribes structure of description, never the architecture itself. Heavy for small ventures.
records.counter_evidence: C4 (EV-0101) and arc42 achieve the same stakeholder-concern discipline with far less ceremony, which is why lighter models dominate practice despite the standard's existence.

records.source: Shopify Engineering, Deconstructing the monolith
records.licence: unknown (Shopify site, no open licence stated)
records.finding: A very large Rails monolith was made tractable without splitting deployables: components with declared public interfaces inside one process, plus an in-house tool (Wedge) that reads call graphs produced by CI runs and scores each component's isolation, listing every boundary violation. Runtime call-graph analysis catches the dynamic violations that static import rules cannot see, and a per-component score turns a migration into something measurable rather than aspirational.
records.applicability_limits: One company, one language with heavy metaprogramming, hundreds of engineers, no counterfactual. The tool is not public. Reported outcomes are qualitative developer-productivity claims.
records.counter_evidence: Progressive scores mean violations are tolerated rather than blocked, which is the opposite of a red-build boundary; the approach fits migration of legacy mass, not a greenfield venture that can refuse violations from day one.

records.source: Uber Engineering, Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture
records.licence: unknown (Uber site, no open licence stated)
records.finding: At roughly 2,200 services the failure mode named was the networked monolith: services that look independent but must be deployed together, with an incident touching about 50 services across 12 teams. The remedy was to reimpose structure, grouping services into around 70 domains, defining five layers with an explicit rule about which layer may call which, and putting a gateway in front of each domain so consumers never bind to internal services.
records.applicability_limits: Extreme scale, single company, self-reported outcomes with no baseline methodology (support cost 'order of magnitude' lower, integration three days to three hours, onboarding 25 to 50 per cent faster). Nothing here is testable at venture scale.
records.counter_evidence: This is a large organisation paying to recover, inside a distributed system, the layering and interface discipline a modular monolith gets for free, which is direct evidence against splitting before the coupling problem is real.

records.source: Stripe documentation, Webhooks and signature verification
records.finding: The vendor seam has hard protocol requirements that a framework can silently break: verification is HMAC-SHA256 over the exact raw request bytes, so any middleware that parses or re-serialises the body destroys the signature; the signed timestamp gives replay protection with a default five-minute tolerance which must never be set to zero; and the event payload shape is pinned to the account's API version at the moment the event was created, not the version the handler uses today.
records.applicability_limits: Stripe specifics. Tolerances, header format and version-pinning semantics differ per vendor, so the rule that transfers is 'verify raw bytes, bound recency, pin payload version', not the constants.
records.counter_evidence: Stripe supplies SDK helpers that do the verification, which softens the case for hand-rolled raw-protocol handling; the durable argument for owning it is that the raw-body requirement is exactly what a framework upgrade breaks.

records.source: Chris Richardson, Database per service pattern (microservices.io)
records.licence: unknown (site copyright, no open licence stated)
records.finding: Data ownership and physical database separation are different decisions. The isolation the pattern wants can be bought at three escalating prices: private tables, a separate schema, or a separate server, with enforcement by distinct database credentials. Taking the cheapest level that enforces the rule preserves joins and single-transaction consistency, while the expensive level forces sagas for writes and API composition or CQRS for reads.
records.applicability_limits: Written for multi-team microservice estates. The drawbacks it lists (cross-service transactions, cross-database joins) are precisely the costs a single-database venture does not pay, so the pattern is a warning label as much as a recommendation.
records.counter_evidence: It labels the shared database a pattern to avoid, yet its own enforcement mechanism (separate credentials on private tables in one database) is a shared database with ownership rules, which shows the anti-pattern label is about uncontrolled access, not about physical colocation.

records.source: Martin Fowler, What do you mean by Event-Driven?
records.finding: Four distinct patterns hide behind the phrase event-driven, and they have different costs: event notification (low coupling, but no explicit flow to read), event-carried state transfer (removes queries, adds replicated state and staleness), event sourcing (log is the truth, gives audit and replay) and CQRS (separate read and write models). The named hazards are that event-sourced replay breaks when handling touched external systems, and that CQRS is frequently misused where a single model would serve.
records.applicability_limits: Definitional essay with no measurement, nine years old, no guidance on volume thresholds or operational cost. Written before ubiquitous managed streaming.
records.counter_evidence: The source's central warning is that failures get blamed on 'event-driven architecture' when the responsible pattern was one of the four, so any pack rule must name the specific pattern or it inherits the same confusion.

records.source: Google Engineering Practices Documentation (eng-practices)
records.population: Google engineering, all languages and projects, distilled from internal guidance
records.version_or_commit: master branch as published at google.github.io/eng-practices; repository archived read-only 2025-11-21
records.licence: CC BY 3.0 (documents); Apache-2.0 for any code
records.finding: Review approves on a health gradient, not a perfection bar: approve once the change definitely improves overall code health even when imperfect, refuse only what definitely worsens it, and separate design judgement (arguable on engineering grounds) from style (settled by the style guide, never by reviewer taste). The author-side guide makes small changes the mechanism that makes this affordable, because reviewers can find five minutes repeatedly but not thirty minutes once.
records.applicability_limits: Written for a very large monorepo with mandatory readability certification, ownership files and dedicated review tooling. A solo or two-person venture has no reviewer pool, so the health-gradient rule transfers but the ownership and readability machinery does not. The repository is archived, so it is a fixed historical artefact and will not track agentic review practice.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0167 argues every stated goal of human review can be met by agents; the archive status is itself weak evidence that Google no longer treats this text as living guidance.
records.review: on-change-of:any successor to google/eng-practices or an un-archive of the repository

records.source: Sadowski, Soderberg, Church, Sipko, Bacchelli, Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google
records.study_design: Exploratory mixed-method case study: interviews, survey and log analysis of Critique review data
records.population: Google engineers and their change-list review logs, circa 2017
records.licence: unknown (author-hosted preprint; IEEE/ACM proceedings copyright applies to the published version)
records.finding: At scale, review converges on small, single-reviewer, low-iteration changes: the majority of changes are small with one reviewer and no comments beyond the approval, around 70 per cent of changes are committed under 24 hours after being sent for review, and over 80 per cent involve at most one round of comment resolution. Review is sustained for education, norm-setting and gatekeeping as much as for defect finding.
records.applicability_limits: Single-company study inside a monorepo with bespoke tooling and a strong ownership culture; the latency and iteration figures are descriptive of that environment, not a target other teams have been shown to achieve. Pre-dates LLM authorship entirely, so nothing here speaks to reviewing machine-written diffs.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0166 finds the defect-finding expectation is largely unmet in a different company; EV-0167 disputes that human review remains the right instrument at all.

records.source: Bacchelli and Bird, Expectations, Outcomes, and Challenges of Modern Code Review
records.study_design: Multi-method: observations, interviews, survey of managers and developers, manual classification of review comments
records.population: Microsoft product teams using tool-based review
records.licence: unknown (publisher-hosted author copy; ICSE 2013 proceedings copyright applies)
records.finding: Expectation and outcome diverge: finding defects is the stated top motivation but reviews yield far fewer defect findings than expected and deliver most of their value as knowledge transfer, team awareness and alternative solutions. The binding constraint on review quality is the reviewer's understanding of the change and its context, which tooling mostly fails to supply.
records.applicability_limits: One large company, 2013 tooling, human-authored code. The understanding constraint is the transferable part; the specific comment-category proportions are not.
records.counter_evidence: If knowledge transfer is the real product, a solo operator with agent authors gets little from ceremonial review, which weakens the case for mandatory review in small ventures.

records.source: The End of Code Review: Coding Agents Supersede Human Inspection
records.study_design: Position and synthesis paper; no new empirical data, argues from published benchmark results
records.population: n/a
records.model: surveys frontier coding agents circa late 2025
records.licence: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive licence to distribute (author copyright retained)
records.finding: The argument that mandatory human review no longer pays is now stated explicitly in the literature: agents can serve defect detection, style enforcement and awareness at lower cost, humans spend a reported 10 to 15 per cent of hours reviewing, and feedback routinely takes over 24 hours. The paper's own concessions are the useful part: hallucinated approvals, non-trivial vulnerability injection rates, unsolved prompt injection, weak architectural judgement, and an accountability gap when an auto-approved change causes harm, so it lands on ensemble review with human oversight reserved for high-risk changes.
records.applicability_limits: Not peer-reviewed and not empirical; it is an argument, not a measurement. Benchmark resolution rates on curated issues do not license claims about review of arbitrary production diffs. Treat as a well-formed hypothesis and as a checklist of the risks any review-automation policy must answer.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0010 (METR RCT) shows measured slowdown where practitioners believed in speed-up, so agent-capability arguments that assume perceived gains are real should be discounted.
records.review: on-change-of:peer-reviewed publication or empirical replacement for this preprint

records.source: DORA capability page, Trunk-based development
records.study_design: Practitioner guidance summarising DORA survey analysis (2016 and 2017 State of DevOps data cited on the page)
records.population: DORA State of DevOps respondents, tens of thousands of professionals across years
records.finding: Trunk-based development is defined operationally by four measurable conditions rather than by ideology: three or fewer active branches, branch lifetime of hours not days, at least one merge to trunk per developer per day, and no code-freeze periods. These are stated as required practice for continuous integration and are associated with higher delivery and operational performance.
records.applicability_limits: Survey-based association, self-reported, not a controlled experiment, and the causal direction is asserted rather than demonstrated. The four thresholds assume a multi-developer team; for a solo or agent-driven repo the meaningful residue is merge cadence and the ban on code freezes, not branch counts.
records.counter_evidence: The page itself concedes that trunk-based development is a substantial change requiring new skills and meets organisational resistance, so adoption cost is real.
records.review: on-change-of:new DORA report revising the trunk-based capability

records.source: DORA, State of AI-assisted Software Development 2025
records.study_design: Annual cross-sectional survey with modelling; self-reported measures
records.population: Software development professionals worldwide, 2025 wave
records.model: AI coding assistants generally, not a named model
records.version_or_commit: 2025 report as published on dora.dev, accessed 2026-08-03
records.finding: AI amplifies the system it lands in rather than fixing it: adoption is near-universal (around 90 per cent), individual output rises sharply (reported figures around 21 per cent more tasks and far more pull requests merged), yet end-to-end delivery performance stays flat where the surrounding process is weak. Trust is low, with roughly a quarter reporting high trust and roughly a third little or none.
records.applicability_limits: Self-report, cross-sectional, no causal identification; the throughput figures measure activity, not delivered value. Aggregated across organisation sizes, so the flat-delivery result is about organisational bottlenecks that a one-person venture does not have in the same form.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0010 (METR RCT) measured a 19 per cent slowdown for experienced developers on their own repositories, directly contradicting self-reported throughput gains.
records.review: on-change-of:publication of the next annual DORA report

records.source: Conventional Commits specification
records.finding: A tiny grammar over commit subjects (type, optional scope, description, optional body and footers, with breaking change signalled by a bang or a BREAKING CHANGE footer) turns history into a machine-readable event stream: changelogs, version bumps and release triggers become derivations rather than manual work. The spec deliberately keeps only feat and fix mandatory and leaves further types to the team.
records.applicability_limits: Buys nothing unless something downstream actually consumes it (release automation, changelog generation, version selection); as decoration it is pure ceremony. Revert semantics are explicitly unspecified. The spec anticipates that not every contributor complies and suggests maintainer normalisation at merge, which matters when commit authors are agents.
records.counter_evidence: The spec's own FAQ concedes the risk that a fixed type vocabulary narrows the kinds of commit developers are willing to make.

records.source: Semantic Versioning specification
records.finding: Version numbers only carry meaning once a public API is declared precisely and comprehensively, in code or in documentation; MAJOR signals incompatible API change, MINOR backward-compatible addition, PATCH backward-compatible fix. Major version zero is an explicit escape hatch where anything may change at any time.
records.applicability_limits: The contract is only as good as the API declaration behind it; without one the numbers are decoration. Says nothing about how to decide compatibility for behavioural or performance changes, which is where most real breakage occurs. Ecosystems (npm ranges, Go modules) layer their own resolution rules on top.
records.counter_evidence: Date-based rolling versions with per-consumer pinning, as in EV-0061 (Stripe API versioning), solve the same coordination problem without semantic compatibility judgements.

records.source: Potvin and Levenberg, Why Google Stores Billions of Lines of Code in a Single Repository
records.study_design: Experience report with operational statistics; no comparison group
records.population: Google's Piper monorepo, reported at roughly 2 billion lines, 40,000 commits per working day, over 10,000 engineers
records.version_or_commit: Communications of the ACM vol 59 no 7 (2016), pages 78-87
records.licence: unknown (ACM copyright; the CACM web version is publicly readable)
records.finding: A monorepo buys one-version dependency management, atomic cross-project change and cheap large-scale refactoring, and it presupposes trunk-based development with essentially no long-lived branches. The report is candid that these benefits are bought with a bespoke tooling investment (Piper, CitC, build and analysis infrastructure) that most organisations cannot fund.
records.applicability_limits: The tooling cost is the whole story; quoting the benefits without the investment is the standard misreading. At venture scale the same benefits are available in a plain git monorepo precisely because the repo is small, so the paper argues for monorepo-by-default only in the small case and monorepo-with-heavy-tooling in the large case, with a painful middle.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0173 catalogues the countervailing costs (tooling, build times, cross-team coupling, unclear ownership) reported by practitioners without Google-scale infrastructure.

records.source: Brito, Terra and Valente, Monorepos: A Multivocal Literature Review
records.study_design: Multivocal literature review, predominantly grey literature
records.population: Practitioner articles and talks on monorepo adoption
records.licence: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive licence (author copyright retained)
records.finding: The monorepo debate resolves into a named trade set rather than a winner: centralisation and standardisation give simplified dependencies, coordinated cross-project change and easy refactoring, and cost tooling investment, slower builds and weaker ownership boundaries. The decision is therefore about which costs you can pay, not which model is correct.
records.applicability_limits: Grey-literature synthesis, so it reports advocacy rather than measurement, and it is eight years old, predating the current generation of build and task tooling and predating agentic authorship entirely.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0172 reports the monorepo benefits realised at extreme scale, which grey literature tends to over-generalise from.
records.review: on-change-of:a controlled or large-sample empirical comparison of monorepo and polyrepo outcomes

records.source: Yuan et al., Simple Testing Can Prevent Most Critical Failures (OSDI 14)
records.study_design: Retrospective manual analysis of 198 randomly sampled user-reported production failures
records.population: Cassandra, HBase, HDFS, Hadoop MapReduce, Redis
records.licence: unknown (USENIX open-access proceedings; USENIX and author copyright)
records.finding: Error handling is where catastrophe lives: 92 per cent of catastrophic failures studied came from incorrect handling of non-fatal errors that the software had already explicitly signalled, and about a third of those were trivial mistakes visible to plain code inspection with no system knowledge. Most failures reproduced on three nodes or fewer.
records.applicability_limits: Java-heavy distributed data systems circa 2014; the proportions are of that corpus. The transferable claim is the direction of attention, that the error path deserves more review and test effort than the happy path, not the exact percentage.
records.counter_evidence: None found that disputes the direction; later work generally reinforces error-path neglect.

records.source: The Go Blog, Working with Errors in Go 1.13
records.version_or_commit: published 2019-10-17, describing Go 1.13 errors.Is, errors.As and fmt.Errorf %w
records.licence: CC BY 4.0 for site content per the go.dev notice; code samples BSD-3-Clause
records.finding: Error identity is an interface decision, not a convenience: wrapping an error makes that error part of the caller-visible API, so wrap deliberately when callers should be able to react to the cause, and convert without wrapping when the cause is an implementation detail you refuse to commit to. Whatever you document as inspectable must always be returned that way, and inspection goes through chain-aware predicates rather than equality on a concrete type.
records.applicability_limits: Go-specific mechanics. The transferable rule is that the set of distinguishable failure modes is part of a module's contract and must be declared and versioned like any other part of it; languages with exceptions or Result types express the same rule differently.
records.counter_evidence: Ecosystems that treat all errors as opaque strings trade caller-side recovery for looser coupling; that is a real position, not an error, in throwaway or leaf code.
records.review: on-change-of:a Go proposal changing error inspection semantics

records.source: Feitelson, Mizrahi, Noy et al., How Developers Choose Names
records.study_design: Sequence of controlled naming experiments with blind analysis of chosen names
records.population: 334 subjects across the experiments, 47 naming instances
records.version_or_commit: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 2021; arXiv:2103.07487v1 preprint
records.licence: unknown (IEEE copyright on the published version; arXiv preprint under arXiv non-exclusive licence)
records.finding: Naming does not converge: the median probability that two developers pick the same name for the same thing was 6.9 per cent, yet a name once chosen is usually understood by most developers. Naming decomposes into choosing which concepts to encode, choosing words for each concept, and assembling them, which is what makes a review comment about a name actionable rather than a taste fight.
records.applicability_limits: Small controlled naming tasks, largely student and professional subjects on short scenarios, not whole-system naming under domain pressure. The asymmetry (low agreement, high comprehension) argues against enforcing name uniformity and for enforcing the concept-selection step.
records.counter_evidence: The high-comprehension result cuts against heavy naming review; if most names are understood anyway, review effort spent on renaming is largely wasted.

records.source: Silva, Tsantalis and Valente, Why We Refactor? Confessions of GitHub Contributors
records.study_design: Firehose monitoring of Java repositories for detected refactorings, followed by developer surveys about each specific refactoring
records.population: GitHub Java projects and their contributors; 44 distinct motivations across 12 refactoring types
records.licence: unknown (ACM copyright on the published version; arXiv preprint under arXiv non-exclusive licence)
records.finding: Refactoring in practice is overwhelmingly change-driven rather than smell-driven: developers refactor to make a specific pending change possible or to remove duplication encountered while working, and the catalogue of 44 motivations is dominated by these situational reasons rather than by detected code smells. This makes smell-detector-driven refactoring backlogs a poor model of how the work actually happens.
records.applicability_limits: Java, open source, 2016, and self-reported motivation with recall and social-desirability bias. Says nothing about whether the refactorings improved anything.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0179 reports refactoring volume collapsing in AI-assisted codebases, which suggests the change-driven trigger is being bypassed rather than that the model is wrong.

records.source: Fucci et al., A Dissection of the Test-Driven Development Process: Does It Really Matter to Test-First or to Test-Last?
records.study_design: Regression modelling of four process characteristics (sequencing, granularity, uniformity, refactoring effort) against quality and productivity
records.population: 82 observations from 39 professional developers
records.version_or_commit: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 2017; arXiv:1611.05994 preprint
records.licence: unknown (IEEE copyright on the published version; arXiv preprint under arXiv non-exclusive licence)
records.finding: The active ingredient in test-driven development is not the sequencing. Quality and productivity were associated with granularity (small uniform work increments) and uniformity (a steady rhythm), not with whether the test came before or after the code. That reframes TDD as a work-decomposition discipline whose test-first ritual is optional scaffolding.
records.applicability_limits: Small sample, short greenfield tasks, human developers in a study setting; effect sizes are modest and the design is correlational within an experimental corpus. It does not license abandoning test-first where regression protection is the goal rather than developer productivity.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0003 (TDAD), EV-0004 (TDFlow), EV-0005 (TDDev) and EV-0007 (risk of coding before testing) all find sequencing matters substantially for agents, where tests supply the oracle the model lacks. The human and agent results are not in conflict once you see that the mechanism differs.

records.source: GitClear, The Maintainability Gap: 2026 AI Code Quality Research
records.study_design: Vendor observational study of git history metrics; non-random convenience sample of customer and public repositories; no control group; full method behind a lead-capture form
records.population: 623 million analysed changes, 2023 to 2026, including repositories owned by large technology firms
records.model: AI coding assistants in aggregate, not attributed per model
records.version_or_commit: January 2026 edition; charts stated to be updated quarterly
records.licence: unknown (no reuse licence stated; site terms of service apply)
records.finding: The measurable signature of AI-assisted codebases is structural rather than functional: refactoring line moves down about 70 per cent, cross-file function calls down about 35 per cent, within-commit copy and paste up about 41 per cent, block duplication up about 81 per cent, error-masking constructs up about 47 per cent, and two-week churn up about 15 per cent. Code gets written and does not get consolidated.
records.applicability_limits: Vendor-run, commercially motivated, sample not random and not disclosed in the public page, metrics are proxies chosen by the vendor and the causal attribution to AI is inferred from timing, not identified. Treat the direction as a hypothesis worth instrumenting locally, never the magnitudes as fact. Note in particular that duplication is not uniformly bad and that a single-owner venture may rationally tolerate more of it.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0169 (DORA 2025) finds delivery outcomes flat rather than degraded, so the structural metrics have not been shown to translate into worse delivered outcomes.
records.review: on-change-of:next quarterly GitClear update or an independent replication

records.source: ApprovalTests.Python
records.version_or_commit: main branch as at 2026-08-03; supports Python 3.10 to 3.14
records.finding: Characterisation testing is mechanised by inverting the assertion: capture current output as an approved artefact, diff every later run against it, and require a human to approve any change. This gets a behaviour net around code nobody understands in minutes, which is exactly the precondition for safe refactoring of inherited or agent-written code.
records.applicability_limits: Approved files lock in current behaviour including current bugs, so they are a refactoring safety net and never a specification. They rot into rubber-stamped diffs unless approval is a deliberate reviewed act. Poor fit for non-deterministic output unless scrubbers are applied.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0094 (write tests, not too many, mostly integration) warns against test volume that does not buy confidence; a large approved-file corpus is precisely that risk if approvals become reflexive.
records.review: on-change-of:a maintenance lapse in the approvals organisation repositories

records.source: Pearce, Ahmad, Tan, Dolan-Gavitt and Karri, Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions
records.study_design: Systematic prompt-completion experiment across diversity of weakness, prompt and domain, with static analysis and manual verification
records.population: 89 security-relevant scenarios producing 1,689 generated programs
records.model: GitHub Copilot (Codex generation, 2021)
records.version_or_commit: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2022; arXiv:2108.09293
records.licence: unknown (IEEE copyright on the published version; arXiv preprint under arXiv non-exclusive licence)
records.finding: Generated code is not security-neutral by default: roughly 40 per cent of generated programs in CWE-relevant scenarios contained a vulnerability, and the rate varied with the weakness class, the prompt and the domain. Prompt context, not model goodwill, is what moves the number.
records.applicability_limits: A 2021 model on deliberately security-loaded scenarios; the headline rate should not be applied to current models or to ordinary code. What survives is the structural claim, that a security gate must sit downstream of generation because generation quality varies with prompt and domain in ways the author cannot see.
records.counter_evidence: Later evaluations of newer models report lower rates; the finding is about the necessity of a gate, not the size of the number.
records.review: on-change-of:a current-model replication of the CWE scenario battery

records.source: Winters, Manshreck and Wright (eds), Software Engineering at Google
records.population: Google engineering practice as narrated by its practitioners
records.version_or_commit: first edition, March 2020, O'Reilly; free digital edition on abseil.io
records.licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (digital edition); no derivatives permitted, so extract principles only and never adapt the text
records.finding: Software engineering is programming integrated over time, so every construction rule should be justified by what it costs to keep the code alive rather than by what it costs to write. The corollaries used in practice are that code is read far more often than written, that expensive review is bought down by keeping changes small and reviewers few, and that any behaviour you want preserved must be defended by an automated test rather than by convention.
records.applicability_limits: No-derivatives licence constrains reuse of the text itself. Practices assume a monorepo, a build system that can run affected tests cheaply, and thousands of engineers; the time-integration principle transfers to a one-person venture but the review and ownership machinery does not.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0089 (harness design, Anthropic) warns that scaffolding encodes assumptions about model weakness and should be stripped as models improve; a long-lived practice corpus is exactly the kind of scaffolding that ossifies.

records.source: trunkbaseddevelopment.com
records.version_or_commit: site as served 2026-08-03; copyright notice reads 2017-2020
records.licence: unknown (no explicit reuse licence found; site copyright Paul Hammant with community contributions)
records.finding: Trunk-based development is specified as a ladder rather than a single practice: small teams commit straight to trunk, scaled teams use short-lived branches that exist only long enough for review and integration, and super-scaled teams add a merge or patch queue. Feature flags and branch by abstraction are the named mechanisms that make large changes compatible with continuous merging, and release branches are temporary and deleted.
records.applicability_limits: Practitioner site, opinion not measurement, and stale by copyright notice. It concedes the small-to-scaled boundary is debated, so the ladder positions are judgement calls. The flag and branch-by-abstraction mechanisms carry their own cost and their own cleanup discipline.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0026 (OpenFeature) shows the flag machinery this model depends on is itself a system needing lifecycle management, which small ventures often skip and then regret.
records.review: on-change-of:a refresh of the site or its replacement by a maintained equivalent

records.source: Martin Fowler, TestDouble bliki entry
records.licence: All rights reserved, copyright Martin Fowler; no reuse licence stated
records.finding: Test double is the umbrella term and the five kinds are not interchangeable: a dummy fills a parameter slot, a stub returns canned answers, a spy is a recording stub, a mock carries pre-programmed expectations that form a specification of calls, and a fake has a real working implementation that takes a production-unsuitable shortcut. Only the fake has behaviour, so only the fake can be held to a behavioural contract.
records.applicability_limits: A vocabulary definition from 2006, not evidence about outcomes; it does not say which double to prefer in which situation and predates modern container and in-memory-emulator tooling. Terminology only, so nothing may be copied verbatim into pack text.

records.source: Martin Fowler, Mocks Aren't Stubs
records.licence: All rights reserved, copyright Martin Fowler; no reuse licence stated
records.finding: The real fork is state verification versus behaviour verification. Classical tests assert on resulting state and use real collaborators where feasible; mockist tests assert on the calls made and therefore couple the test to how the unit does its work, so internal refactoring breaks tests that ought to pass. Choosing a double is choosing what the test is allowed to notice.
records.applicability_limits: A design argument by a named practitioner, not controlled evidence, and last revised in 2007; Fowler himself reports the community never converged. It does not quantify how often mockist coupling actually costs a team.
records.counter_evidence: The mockist school holds that expectation-driven design improves interface discovery and gives sharper failure localisation than state assertions on large object graphs; Fowler records this position without refuting it.

records.source: Martin Fowler, ContractTest bliki entry
records.licence: All rights reserved, copyright Martin Fowler; no reuse licence stated
records.finding: A double is only safe if something proves it still matches the real thing: run a separate contract suite that checks the same calls return the same shapes against the real service, on a slower cadence than the unit suite, and treat a contract failure as an investigation trigger rather than an automatic build break. Sharing that suite with the provider turns it into a consumer-driven contract.
records.applicability_limits: Prescriptive practice guidance, no measured effect size; assumes a reachable test instance of the external service and says format rather than data values is what is checked, so semantic drift inside a stable shape is not caught.
records.counter_evidence: Fowler's advice not to break the build on contract failure conflicts with the Pact deploy-gate model in EV-0091, which makes contract state a hard machine-checked release gate.

records.source: Software Engineering at Google, chapter 13, Test Doubles
records.version_or_commit: O'Reilly 2020 edition, online HTML as read 2026-08-03
records.finding: A stated preference order for doubles: real implementation first when it is fast, deterministic and has simple dependencies; then a fake, which must hold fidelity to the API contract so the same inputs give the same outputs and state changes; then narrow stubbing to force a state; and interaction testing last, because it exposes implementation details. The fake should be written and maintained by the team that owns the real implementation, and the fake is itself tested by running one identical contract suite against both the fake and the real implementation.
records.applicability_limits: Practice from a monorepo with a large infrastructure team and an internal culture that funds API owners to ship fakes; a small venture with third-party SaaS dependencies rarely gets an owner-maintained fake and must write and verify its own. No-derivatives licence, so this must be paraphrased, never adapted or excerpted at length.
records.counter_evidence: Testcontainers (EV-0093) argues the opposite default for infrastructure dependencies, preferring real containerised services over any fake because fakes behave slightly differently; the two agree only that a hand-written mock is the worst option.

records.source: fast-check, property-based testing rationale and repository
records.version_or_commit: docs page last updated 2026-02-07; repository dubzzz/fast-check, v4 line current at access
records.finding: Property-based testing in the JavaScript and TypeScript stack is mature and carries the same three affordances as the Python tooling: generation over a declared input domain, automatic shrinking of a failing case down to a minimal one, and a printed seed plus a global constant-seed option that makes any failure exactly replayable. Determinism is a configuration choice, so a property suite can be made CI-safe rather than randomly red.
records.applicability_limits: Documentation from the maintainer with no independent evaluation; shrinking quality depends on how arbitraries are composed, and a constant seed trades away the exploration that motivates the technique, so seed policy has to be decided per suite.

records.source: Schemathesis
records.version_or_commit: stable docs build as read 2026-08-03; supports OpenAPI 2.0, 3.0, 3.1, 3.2 and GraphQL
records.finding: An interface schema is already a machine-readable property specification: driving Hypothesis-style generation straight off an OpenAPI or GraphQL document tests conformance and negative paths that hand-written example tests skip, and every finding ships with a minimal curl reproducer, so the schema doubles as the oracle and the bug report.
records.applicability_limits: Vendor documentation; the claim of commonly five to fifteen findings per production schema is a maintainer estimate with no published method or sample. It only checks conformance to the declared schema, so a wrong-but-well-described API passes, and it needs a running service.

records.source: StrykerJS thresholds configuration
records.version_or_commit: StrykerJS configuration docs, 7.x and later, as read 2026-08-03
records.finding: Mutation score becomes a gate only when a break threshold is set: high defaults to 80 and low to 60 for reporting colour, while break defaults to null, meaning the tool reports but never fails a build until someone deliberately sets a number, at which point a score below it exits non-zero. The tool ships an opinionated reporting band and an unopinionated gate, so the pack must supply the gate number itself.
records.applicability_limits: Configuration reference for the JavaScript runner; the 80 and 60 bands are stated defaults with no published justification and no evidence they transfer across languages or codebase maturity. Full-run cost still governs whether a per-commit gate is affordable.

records.source: Just, Jalali, Inozemtseva, Ernst, Holmes, Fraser, Are mutants a valid substitute for real faults in software testing? (FSE 2014)
records.study_design: Empirical coupling study over real faults reproduced from open-source history, with developer-written and automatically generated suites
records.population: 357 real faults across 5 open-source Java applications, roughly 321,000 lines of code, evaluated against mutants from 31 mutation operators
records.version_or_commit: FSE 2014 proceedings, pages 654 to 665; author-hosted PDF as read 2026-08-03
records.licence: unknown (author-hosted preprint of an ACM paper)
records.finding: 73% of real faults were coupled to at least one mutant, and mutant detection correlated with real-fault detection independently of code coverage, which is the primary evidence that mutation score is a better proxy for fault-finding than coverage. Conditional and relational operator replacement and statement deletion coupled most often, so operator choice matters more than mutant count.
records.applicability_limits: Java, five projects, faults drawn from version-control history and therefore biased towards faults that were found and fixed; 27% of real faults were coupled to no mutant at all, so a perfect mutation score does not imply a fault-free suite.
records.counter_evidence: The same paper reports that when test-suite size is controlled the correlation between mutant detection and real-fault detection becomes weak, which means a high mutation score achieved by adding volume rather than by adding oracles proves little.

records.source: Petrović and Ivanković et al, Practical Mutation Testing at Scale: a view from Google
records.study_design: Industrial deployment report on a code-review-integrated mutation service
records.population: More than 24,000 developers across more than 1,000 projects in a two-billion-line monorepo running over 500 million tests daily
records.finding: Mutation testing becomes affordable at any scale by refusing to mutate most of the code: mutate only the diff, skip lines with no statement coverage, suppress arid lines that carry no interesting behaviour, and filter by context before surfacing anything. Surfacing a small number of high-quality mutants inside code review, rather than a score in a nightly report, is what makes the signal actionable.
records.applicability_limits: A deployment report from a monorepo with uniform tooling and a mandatory review culture, not a controlled comparison; the arid-line heuristics are tuned to Google's own libraries, and the abstract gives no numeric actionability rate.
records.counter_evidence: Follow-up work by the same group reports that only about 38% of surfaced mutants, and 60% of those judged productive, lead to a code or test change, so most surfaced mutants still cost reviewer attention without changing anything.

records.source: Pact can-i-deploy and the Pact Matrix
records.licence: unknown (docs.pact.io site, Pact Foundation copyright; Pact tooling itself MIT)
records.finding: Contract testing only pays off when it terminates in a machine-answerable release question. The broker records every consumer and provider version pair that has been verified, can-i-deploy queries that matrix for the environment being targeted and exits zero or one, and record-deployment writes back what is actually live so the next query is asked against reality rather than against a wiki page.
records.applicability_limits: The gate is only as honest as the recorded deployments; a service deployed outside the pipeline makes the matrix stale and the gate falsely green. It answers compatibility of recorded interactions only, never behavioural correctness, and the page has not been revised since 2022.
records.counter_evidence: Fowler's ContractTest guidance argues a contract failure should trigger investigation rather than block, which is the opposite disposition to a hard exit-code deploy gate.

records.source: Develocity Predictive Test Selection user manual
records.licence: Proprietary, commercial Develocity extension; docs copyright Gradle Inc
records.finding: Mature test-impact analysis is a predicted subset plus a guaranteed floor plus a settlement run. Tests that are new, changed, recently failed or recently flaky are always selected whatever the model says; a confidence profile trades detection against saved time; a simulator scores the policy on historical builds before anyone trusts it; and the selected subset runs pre-merge while the remainder runs post-merge, so every test still runs once per changeset.
records.applicability_limits: A paid extension for Gradle and Maven JVM builds whose model is trained on the customer's own build-scan history, so it needs volume before it predicts well and does not transfer to small or young repositories. Vendor documentation with no independent evaluation of missed-failure rates.
records.counter_evidence: Playwright's --only-changed (EV-0016) achieves cheap selection from the import graph with no model, no service and no data history, which suggests the machine-learning layer is a scale optimisation rather than a requirement.

records.source: John Micco, Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them (Google Testing Blog)
records.licence: unknown (Google Testing Blog, no reuse licence stated on page)
records.finding: Flake is managed as a named state with an explicit policy rather than by blanket retries: reruns apply only to tests already marked flaky or on request, chronically flaky tests are quarantined out of the blocking path into a reliability suite, and flakiness is monitored per test and per configuration so the same test can be flaky under one flag set and sound under another.
