records.study_design: Observational audit of Chatbot Arena battle data, sampling rates, private variant testing and model removals, plus an experiment on the effect of additional arena data on arena performance
records.population: Arena-listed models from proprietary and open-weight providers
records.finding: A public leaderboard is a measurement system with its own incentives, and those incentives distort it. Undisclosed private testing lets a provider run many variants and publish only the best, sampling rates and data access are heavily skewed towards a few large providers, and modest amounts of extra arena-distribution data produced relative gains of up to 112 per cent on the arena itself, which is overfitting to the leaderboard rather than improvement. The decision rule is that leaderboard position never justifies a model choice on its own: choose on a private task-specific evaluation, and treat public rankings as a shortlist generator.
records.applicability_limits: One leaderboard, one measurement period, and an observational audit whose estimates of data share are inferred rather than supplied by the operator. The arena operators dispute parts of the account. The overfitting experiment shows arena-specific gains, not that the models are worse in general. None of this transfers automatically to task-specific benchmarks with fixed hidden test sets.
records.counter_evidence: The Chatbot Arena maintainers published a rebuttal contesting the characterisation of private testing and of sampling policy, and others argue the arena remains the best available broad preference signal. This disagreement is unresolved at cutoff.
records.licence_evidence: Abstract page shows the by-sa-4.0 licence icon with "view license" linking to http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/ titled "Rights to this article" (title: The Leaderboard Illusion)

records.source: Chen, Zaharia and Zou, How Is ChatGPT's Behavior Changing over Time? (Harvard Data Science Review, 2024)
records.study_design: Longitudinal re-measurement of the same task battery against two dated snapshots of the same commercial model endpoints
records.population: Seven task families including arithmetic, sensitive questions, opinion surveys, multi-hop QA, code generation, medical licensing questions and visual reasoning
records.model: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, March 2023 and June 2023 snapshots
records.finding: The same model name behind the same endpoint can change behaviour substantially in months, and the changes are not uniformly improvements: one prime-versus-composite task fell from 84 per cent to 51 per cent between two snapshots, and instruction-following degraded noticeably. The decision rule is that a model endpoint is an unstable dependency: pin dated model identifiers rather than moving aliases, run your regression suite against the pinned version and the candidate version before migrating, and keep continuous monitoring because behaviour can move without any change on your side.
records.applicability_limits: Two snapshots of one vendor's models in 2023, and the arithmetic result in particular was criticised on the grounds that the June model's answers changed format rather than becoming uniformly worse, so part of the measured drop is a parsing artefact. It shows that drift can happen, not how often it happens now. Providers have since published clearer deprecation and pinning policies, see EV-0260.
records.counter_evidence: Contemporary reanalyses argued the headline arithmetic collapse partly reflected changed output formatting and chain-of-thought behaviour rather than lost capability, so the magnitude is contested even though the phenomenon is real.
records.review: on-change-of:a longitudinal drift study on current pinned endpoints

records.source: Anthropic, Model deprecations (Claude platform documentation)
records.version_or_commit: Page state as fetched 2026-08-03, listing claude-opus-4-1-20250805 deprecated 2026-06-05 with retirement 2026-08-05
records.licence: proprietary vendor documentation, no open licence stated; paraphrase only
records.finding: A frontier provider publishes an explicit four-state model lifecycle (active, legacy, deprecated, retired), commits to at least sixty days' notice before retiring a publicly released model, publishes tentative retirement dates for active models roughly a year or more out, and provides a usage export so a customer can audit which keys still call a deprecated model. Requests to a retired model fail outright. It also deprecates API parameters: temperature, top_p and top_k now return a 400 on the newest model line. The decision rule is that model choice carries a scheduled expiry: record the pinned model id and its published retirement date next to the code that calls it, hold a migration evaluation ready, and run a usage audit before every retirement date rather than discovering the failure in production.
records.applicability_limits: One vendor. Partner-operated platforms such as Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud set their own schedules, so a multi-cloud deployment has several different clocks. Sixty days is a floor, not a comfortable migration window for a system with a large evaluation suite. Retirement dates for active models are explicitly tentative, so they cannot be treated as contractual. The page is live and changes without notice, so a cited state is a snapshot.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0259 shows behaviour can move within a pinned name's lifetime, so a documented lifecycle policy bounds the availability risk without eliminating the behavioural drift risk.

records.source: Anthropic, Prompt caching (Claude platform documentation)
records.version_or_commit: Page state as fetched 2026-08-03: cache write 1.25x base input for the 5 minute TTL and 2x for the 1 hour TTL, cache read 0.1x base input, minimum cacheable prefix between 512 and 4096 tokens depending on model
records.licence: proprietary vendor documentation, no open licence stated; paraphrase only
records.finding: Cost and latency are architectural choices made in prompt layout, not just in model choice. Cached prefix reads are charged at a tenth of base input while writes cost a quarter to a full multiple more, so a stable prefix that is reused several times pays for itself quickly and an unstable one loses money. Minimum cacheable length varies by model and short prompts silently fail to cache with no error, so the only reliable check is reading cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens back from the response. Cache hits also do not count against rate limits. The decision rule is to order every prompt stable-prefix-first, variable-suffix-last, and to assert cache hit rate in production telemetry rather than assuming caching is on.
records.applicability_limits: One vendor's pricing and mechanics; multipliers, minimums and TTL options differ across providers and change without notice, so any number here must be re-read before it is used in a cost model. The documentation states no quantified latency reduction, so time-to-first-token gains must be measured on your own workload. Caching helps only where the prefix genuinely repeats, which excludes highly personalised single-shot prompts.
records.counter_evidence: The stable-prefix discipline pulls against the retrieval discipline in EV-0243, which wants the most relevant evidence near the edges of the context; caching wants the invariant material first, so the two rules must be reconciled deliberately.
records.review: on-change-of:the Anthropic prompt caching pricing table

records.source: Chen, Zaharia and Zou, FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance
records.study_design: Design and evaluation of a learned cascade router over a heterogeneous set of commercial LLM APIs, measured on cost against accuracy
records.population: Question answering and classification datasets priced against commercial API tariffs
records.model: Twelve commercial APIs available in 2023, including GPT-4 and cheaper alternatives
records.finding: Model prices differ by around two orders of magnitude, so routing is a first-class cost lever. A cascade that tries a cheap model first, scores its own answer with a learned confidence function, and escalates only on low confidence matched the best single model's accuracy at up to 98 per cent lower cost in the reported settings. The generalisable rules are the three levers named: adapt the prompt (shorter context, fewer demonstrations), approximate the model (cache, distil), and cascade across models. The decision rule is to design the escalation policy and measure its escalation rate, because that rate is the actual cost dial.
records.applicability_limits: 2023 model line-up and 2023 tariffs, and the headline 98 per cent figure is dataset-specific and should never be quoted as a general expectation. The cascade needs a trained scorer and labelled data to train it, which is real engineering cost that the paper's savings figures do not carry. It predates prompt caching and batch pricing, which now capture part of the same saving with far less machinery. Cascades add latency on escalated queries and add a second failure mode when the scorer is wrong.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0245's Self-Route achieves comparable routing benefit using the model's own self-assessment with no trained scorer, which suggests the trained cascade may be more machinery than most ventures need.
records.licence_evidence: Abstract page shows "view license" linking to http://arxiv.org/licenses/nonexclusive-distrib/1.0/ with title attribute "Rights to this article" (title: FrugalGPT: How to Use Large Language Models While Reducing Cost and Improving Performance)

records.source: Tam and colleagues, Let Me Speak Freely? A Study on the Impact of Format Restrictions on Performance of Large Language Models (EMNLP 2024 Industry Track)
records.study_design: Controlled comparison of free-form generation against format-restricted generation (JSON, XML, YAML) and against constrained decoding, across reasoning and classification tasks
records.population: Reasoning and classification task suites
records.model: Contemporary open and closed chat models
records.benchmark: GSM8K, Last Letter Concatenation, Shuffled Objects, plus classification sets
records.finding: Forcing structured output is not free. Reasoning accuracy fell under format restriction, and the tighter the constraint the larger the drop, with constrained decoding worse than a natural-language instruction to produce the format. The reported mitigation is to separate the two jobs: let the model reason in free text, then convert to the required schema in a second cheap call. The decision rule is that a structured-output requirement is a design decision with a measurable quality cost, so any pipeline that emits JSON directly from a reasoning step should carry an eval comparing it against reason-then-convert.
records.applicability_limits: 2024 models, and vendors have since invested heavily in native structured output and tool calling, so the size of the penalty on current models is unestablished and may be small or absent. Findings were contested by maintainers of constrained-decoding libraries who argued the prompts used were not the recommended ones for their tools, so part of the gap may be prompt quality rather than constraint. Classification tasks showed less degradation than reasoning tasks.
records.counter_evidence: Maintainers of Outlines and Instructor publicly disputed the constrained-decoding comparison as unrepresentative of correct usage; this disagreement is not resolved at cutoff and is a reason to treat the effect as must-measure rather than as settled.
records.licence_evidence: Abstract page shows "view license" linking to http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/ (title: Let Me Speak Freely? A Study on the Impact of Format Restrictions on Performance of Large Language Models)

records.source: UK AI Security Institute, Inspect: a framework for large language model evaluations
records.version_or_commit: main branch as inspected 2026-08-03; distributed on PyPI as inspect-ai on the 0.3.x line
records.finding: A national safety institute's evaluation framework settles on a small set of first-class nouns: a dataset of samples, a solver that produces the output (including multi-turn and tool-using solvers), and a scorer that grades it, with a viewer for inspecting individual transcripts. Evaluation is therefore a versioned artefact in the repository with the same lifecycle as code, and model-graded scoring is one scorer type among several rather than the default. The companion inspect_evals collection ships over two hundred pre-built evaluations. The decision rule is to adopt the dataset-solver-scorer separation whatever tool you use, because it is what lets you swap the model without rewriting the eval and swap the scorer without rewriting the dataset.
records.applicability_limits: Built for safety and capability evaluation of models, so the abstractions fit model comparison better than they fit end-to-end product evaluation with a live retrieval corpus and real user traffic. Python only. The 0.3.x line is pre-1.0 and the API has changed across minor versions, so pinning is required. Being government-funded is not a guarantee of long-term maintenance.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0265 and EV-0266 encode different decompositions of the same problem, so the dataset-solver-scorer split is one defensible shape rather than a standard.
records.review: on-change-of:a 1.0 release or an archive of inspect_ai

records.source: Ragas, evaluation toolkit for LLM applications
records.version_or_commit: main branch as inspected 2026-08-03, approximately 15.1k stars
records.finding: The most widely adopted RAG evaluation toolkit decomposes quality along axes that attribute failure to a stage: faithfulness and answer relevance for the generation step, context precision and context recall for the retrieval step. That decomposition is the durable idea, because a single end-to-end score cannot tell you whether to fix the retriever or the prompt. Several of its metrics are reference-free, computed by a judge model against the question and retrieved context rather than against a gold answer, which is what makes continuous measurement affordable.
records.applicability_limits: Reference-free metrics are judge-model outputs and inherit every bias in EV-0251 to EV-0253, so the scores are only meaningful once calibrated against a human-labelled sample. The metric definitions have changed across major versions and the library has repeatedly reshaped its API, so scores are not comparable across upgrades without re-baselining. Running the metrics costs model calls, which is a real ongoing spend. Vendor-adjacent open source with a commercial product behind it.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0254 argues criteria must be derived from your own graded outputs, which cuts against adopting a fixed four-metric vocabulary as if it were the definition of quality.
records.review: on-change-of:a major version of ragas that redefines the core metrics

records.source: Stanford NLP, DSPy: programming, not prompting, language models
records.version_or_commit: 3.x line as inspected 2026-08-03, approximately 34k stars; underlying paper arXiv:2310.03714
records.finding: Prompts can be treated as compiled artefacts rather than as handwritten strings. A declared signature states the input and output fields, a module states the strategy, and an optimiser searches instructions and demonstrations against a metric on a training set, so the object under version control is the program and the metric rather than the prompt text. This is the strongest available answer to the prompt brittleness in EV-0256: if the prompt is generated against a measured objective, formatting choices stop being folklore. The decision rule is that once a prompt has an eval set and more than a handful of tuned variants, hand-tuning is the more expensive option.
records.applicability_limits: Requires a metric and a labelled training set before it can do anything, so it is useless at the stage where a team does not yet know what good looks like. Optimisation consumes model calls, sometimes a lot of them. The optimiser menu changes fast and results are optimiser-specific, so a compiled program is tied to a library version and a model version and must be recompiled when either moves. Adds a substantial abstraction layer that makes debugging a bad output harder for a small team.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0086 and EV-0087 describe Anthropic's practice as direct, legible context engineering with human-written instructions, which is a materially different philosophy: legibility and debuggability over compiled optimality. Neither side has a controlled comparison at cutoff.
records.review: on-change-of:a DSPy 4.x release or a major optimiser deprecation

records.source: MLCommons, AILuminate: Introducing v1.0 of the AI Risk and Reliability Benchmark
records.study_design: Consortium-built safety benchmark: a hazard taxonomy, an assessment standard, and a private-plus-public prompt split scored by an ensemble of evaluator models, graded on a five-point scale
records.population: General-purpose chat systems
records.benchmark: AILuminate v1.0 and v1.1, twelve hazard categories, over 24,000 prompts per language split 12,000 public practice and 12,000 private official
records.version_or_commit: arXiv:2503.05731, March 2025; prompt and tooling repository at github.com/mlcommons/ailuminate covering v1.1
records.finding: Safety evaluation can be given the same shape as any other release gate: a published hazard taxonomy, an explicit assessment standard defining what counts as a violating response, a public practice set you may tune against, and a private official set you may not, with results reported as ordinal grades from Poor to Excellent rather than as a single number. The public-private split is the load-bearing design choice, because a safety benchmark you can train against stops measuring safety, which is the contamination problem of EV-0257 applied to harm. The decision rule is that a venture keeps its own private safety prompt set, never uses it for tuning, and reports per-hazard grades rather than an aggregate.
records.applicability_limits: Scoped to general-purpose text chat and to twelve named hazards, so it does not cover agentic harms such as unauthorised tool use or exfiltration, which are the categories that matter for the systems this estate builds; EV-0212 and EV-0213 cover that ground. Grades are produced by an evaluator model ensemble, so they carry judge error. Consortium membership includes the vendors being graded. English-first, with other languages at varying maturity.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0214 and EV-0215 show adaptive attackers break defences that pass static evaluation, so a good AILuminate grade is evidence about refusal behaviour under a fixed prompt distribution and not evidence of robustness.
records.licence_evidence: Abstract page shows the by-4.0 licence icon (arxiv.org/icons/licenses/by-4.0.png) with "view license" linking to http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ (title: AILuminate: Introducing v1.0 of the AI Risk and Reliability Benchmark from MLCommons)

records.source: European Commission, General-Purpose AI Code of Practice and the Article 53 and 55 obligations of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
records.version_or_commit: Final Code of Practice published July 2025; GPAI obligations applicable from 2 August 2025; Commission enforcement powers from 2 August 2026
records.finding: The Code splits into three chapters: Transparency and Copyright bind all providers of general-purpose AI models under Article 53, and Safety and Security binds only providers of models with systemic risk under Article 55. Adherence is voluntary but is the designated route to demonstrating compliance, which makes it the de facto documentation standard. For a venture that builds on models rather than training them, the direct obligations are limited, but the transparency chapter defines the model documentation a provider must supply downstream, so it tells you what you are entitled to receive and therefore what you can record about your dependencies. The decision rule is that model provenance, training-data copyright posture and documented capability limits belong in the venture's dependency record, not in a compliance folder opened once a year.
records.applicability_limits: EU law, and the obligations discussed fall on model providers rather than on downstream deployers, whose duties sit elsewhere in the Act and in the separate high-risk regime. Voluntary adherence means signature does not equal conformity, and the enforcement track record is empty at cutoff since Commission enforcement only opened on 2 August 2026. Interpretation is still moving through Commission guidelines. This record is a paraphrase of policy structure and is not legal advice.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0041 (ICO guidance) and EV-0225 (Data (Use and Access) Act 2025) govern the UK position, which diverges, so a UK venture selling into the EU carries two overlapping regimes rather than one.
records.review: on-change-of:a Commission enforcement decision or a revision of the GPAI Code of Practice
records.licence_evidence: "The General-Purpose AI Code of Practice | Shaping Europe's digital future" states no licence or reuse terms on the page. A scan of the rendered page for "licence/license/Creative Commons/CC BY/reuse" found no licence statement; all "copyright" matches are about the Code's Copyright chapter, not page terms. The footer offers only links named "Copyright notice", "Legal notice", "Privacy statement".

records.source: Vaughn Vernon, Effective Aggregate Design (three-part DDD community essay)
records.version_or_commit: three-part series published 2011; landing page carries copyright 2016-2018 Domain Language, Inc.; Part I PDF Vernon_2011_1.pdf inspected 2026-08-03
records.licence: unknown (Domain Language, Inc. and contributors copyright; no open licence stated on the library page or the PDFs)
records.finding: An aggregate boundary is a transactional consistency boundary, and the only thing that justifies putting two things inside it is an invariant that must never be observed broken. Everything else belongs outside and is reconciled by eventual consistency through domain events. The practical rules that fall out are: modify one aggregate per transaction, hold references to other aggregates by identity only, and prefer small aggregates because large object clusters cost concurrency and load time without buying correctness.
records.applicability_limits: Consulting experience distilled into rules of thumb, with no measurement and no stated population. The central test, whether a rule is a true invariant, is a business decision about tolerable staleness that the essay cannot make for you. Assumes a transactional store and an object-oriented persistence layer; says nothing about analytical or streaming shapes.
records.counter_evidence: Part III of the same series is an account of first aggregate designs being wrong and superseded through discovery, which cuts against any rule that asks for aggregate boundaries to be fixed early or treated as stable interfaces.
records.review: on-change-of:a controlled or large-sample study of aggregate sizing and defect or contention outcomes

records.source: ddd-crew Aggregate Design Canvas
records.version_or_commit: v1.1; 35 commits on main as at 2026-08-03
records.finding: An aggregate design becomes reviewable, and therefore checkable, when it is written down as a fixed set of named fields: enforced invariants, handled commands, created events, state transitions, corrective policies, expected throughput and expected size. The field set is diagnostic as well as descriptive: a long list of corrective policies signals that logic which should sit inside the boundary has leaked into compensating handlers, and a large size or long lifetime signals a boundary that will not load or archive cleanly.
records.applicability_limits: A human workshop artefact under CC BY, so it may be paraphrased and adapted but its wording must not be lifted. The throughput and size prompts assume an event-sourced or event-emitting store; they are meaningless for a plain state-stored aggregate. No evidence exists that the canvas works as an agent-readable input without adaptation.

records.source: EventStorming (Alberto Brandolini, Avanscoperta)
records.version_or_commit: site inspected 2026-08-03, carrying copyright 2025 Avanscoperta S.r.l.
records.licence: unknown (site copyright, all rights reserved; the name EventStorming is claimed as the originator's mark and no open licence is stated)
records.finding: Domain discovery moves faster when the unit of conversation is a past-tense business event rather than an entity, a screen or a table, because an event is a thing every stakeholder can confirm or deny without knowing the software. The format also declares four distinct scopes, from whole-ecosystem exploration down to designing one event-driven service, and picking the wrong scope is the usual reason a session produces nothing usable.
records.applicability_limits: A facilitated workshop that needs domain experts present and a facilitator who can keep the wall honest. The site is also marketing for paid training, so its claims of effectiveness are self-interested. Nothing here transfers directly to an agent working alone from a repository, and no controlled comparison against interviews or ordinary requirements work is offered.
records.counter_evidence: The technique's evidence base is entirely practitioner-authored; the systematic review in EV-0286 finds that DDD-adjacent studies frequently lack empirical evaluation at all.
records.review: on-change-of:a controlled comparison of collaborative event modelling against conventional requirements elicitation

records.source: Martin Fowler, AnemicDomainModel
records.licence: Copyright Martin Fowler, all rights reserved; paraphrase only
records.finding: The failure mode is not having services, it is having objects with no behaviour and services holding all the rules while still paying the full mapping and lifecycle cost of a domain model. The decision rule is a cost test rather than a style test: if you are paying for a domain model, put the rules where the data is; if the rules are thin, do not build the model at all. A procedural service layer over a behaviourally rich model is explicitly fine.
records.applicability_limits: An opinion piece from 2003 with no measurement, written against Java and .NET enterprise practice of that era. It does not tell you where the threshold sits, and it concedes that a domain model is not always the right tool. Functional and data-oriented designs that deliberately separate data from behaviour fall outside its frame.
records.counter_evidence: The same author notes that many respected practitioners recommend a procedural service layer, so a blanket ban on logic outside entities would overreach the source.

records.source: Martin Fowler, Yagni
records.licence: Copyright Martin Fowler, all rights reserved; paraphrase only
records.finding: Speculative capability carries four separate costs, and only the first is obvious: the cost of building it, the delay to work that was actually needed, the carry cost of every future change having to route around it, and the repair cost when the guess turns out wrong. This is the sharpest available argument against over-modelling, because a speculative aggregate, an unused rule engine or a premature bitemporal schema is a carry cost paid on every subsequent change. The stated exception matters: the principle does not apply when the addition costs no extra complexity, nor to investment in the malleability that makes deferring safe.
records.applicability_limits: An argument, not a measurement. It presumes a codebase malleable enough that deferring is cheap; where change is expensive the calculus inverts and the essay says so. It gives no way to tell a genuinely needed abstraction from a speculative one at the moment of decision.
records.counter_evidence: Domain modelling investment is partly an investment in malleability, which is the case the essay itself carves out, so YAGNI cannot be quoted as a blanket argument against modelling.

records.source: Martin Fowler, RulesEngine
records.licence: Copyright Martin Fowler, all rights reserved; paraphrase only
records.finding: Production rule systems trade explicit control flow for implicit interaction, and that trade is what makes them hard to change: chaining, where one rule's action satisfies another rule's condition, produces consequences nobody predicted from reading any single rule. The stated tell is self-defeating: if the rule set is large enough to need a clever matching algorithm for performance, it is already too large to reason about. The recommendation is a small purpose-built rule evaluator inside a narrow context rather than a general engine, and the claim that business people will maintain the rules themselves is named as the thing that usually fails.
records.applicability_limits: Seventeen years old and pre-dates the maturity of DMN-based decision services, which constrain evaluation far more tightly than free-form production rules; the critique lands hardest on chaining engines and least on flat decision tables. No measurement, no population.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0277 and 10 show a standardised, non-chaining decision-table form with defined evaluation semantics, which answers the interaction-complexity objection without abandoning externalised rules.

records.source: Martin Fowler, Patterns for things that change with time
records.licence: Copyright Martin Fowler, all rights reserved; paraphrase only
records.finding: Any domain where a fact can be corrected after the fact needs two time dimensions, not one: when the thing was true in the world, and when the system came to believe it. Without the second, you can answer what the rate is now but not what we thought it was when we ran the payroll, which is the question audits, disputes and reprocessing always ask. The escalation is ordered by cost: an audit log records cheaply but reconstructs expensively; effectivity dating makes validity explicit at the price of every reader knowing about time; temporal property hides the date behind an accessor; a full temporal object versions the whole thing.
records.applicability_limits: Twenty-one years old, illustrative rather than measured, and the pattern names have not become universal vocabulary. It gives no rule for when the second time dimension is worth its cost, which is the decision that actually matters. Storage-engine support, notably system-versioned tables, has changed the economics since publication.
records.counter_evidence: The source concedes that explicit effectivity complicates every model that touches it, so bitemporality by default would be exactly the over-modelling EV-0273 warns about.

records.source: Martin Fowler, Event Sourcing (eaaDev)
records.licence: Copyright Martin Fowler, all rights reserved; paraphrase only
records.finding: Event sourcing buys rebuild, temporal query, replay and audit, and it charges for them in three specific places that are easy to miss when adopting it. Replay must not re-fire external effects, so every outbound call needs a gateway that knows it is replaying. Replay must not re-read external data at today's values, so any external answer used in a decision has to be recorded with the event. And event shapes change, so old events must stay readable forever or be upgraded deliberately. The stated non-reason to adopt is audit alone, which a log gives you more cheaply.
records.applicability_limits: A pattern description from 2005 with no operational data on cost at scale, no guidance on snapshot cadence and no treatment of privacy erasure obligations against an immutable log, which is now a first-order constraint in the UK and EU. Written before managed event stores were ordinary.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0163 by the same author warns that failures get attributed to event-driven architecture in general when one of four distinct patterns was responsible, so event sourcing must be named separately from event notification and CQRS in any rule.

records.source: OMG Decision Model and Notation (DMN)
records.version_or_commit: formal version 1.5, adopted August 2024; version 1.7 beta available for information as at 2026-08-03
records.licence: OMG specification licence, RF-Limited IPR mode; copyright 2026 Object Management Group
records.finding: There is a standard, executable way to express a decision that is not code and not an untyped spreadsheet: a decision requirements graph showing which decisions depend on which inputs and knowledge sources, plus decision tables whose logic is written in a defined expression language (FEEL). The point of the standard for us is not the tooling, it is that a decision table is a closed form with declared inputs, declared outputs and declared overlap handling, so completeness and ambiguity are machine-checkable in a way a chain of if-statements is not.
records.applicability_limits: Adoption is concentrated in enterprise BPM stacks; the standard is large and only a subset is commonly implemented. The claim that business stakeholders can read and own the models is the standard's own assertion and is contested by EV-0274. I confirmed from the OMG specification page that DMN provides the notation, decision tables and FEEL, but did not verify the individual decision-table hit policies at this access, so no rule should name them without a further read of the formal 1.5 document.
records.counter_evidence: Adopting DMN adds a second execution engine and a second artefact to version and test, which for a handful of rules is a clear case of the carry cost in EV-0273.

records.source: Apache KIE Drools
records.version_or_commit: main branch at 2026-08-03, roughly 49,500 commits; project under Apache incubation as incubator-kie-drools
records.finding: A production-grade rule stack in practice bundles three separable things: a forward-chaining Rete engine, a DMN decision engine, and a rule language of its own. They are separable, and that separation is the useful decision: you can take the declarative decision tables without taking inference and chaining, which is where the maintenance objection in EV-0274 actually bites.
records.applicability_limits: JVM only, and heavyweight: adopting it means adopting a runtime, an authoring story and a deployment story. Still in Apache incubation rather than a graduated top-level project, so governance is not yet settled. Nothing here is evidence that externalised rules outperform code, only that mature tooling exists.
records.review: on-change-of:Apache incubation graduation or a change of DMN engine support

records.source: XState (Stately)
records.version_or_commit: main branch at 2026-08-03, roughly 6,965 commits; exact release tag not captured at this access
records.finding: Where a domain object has a lifecycle, encoding that lifecycle as an explicit statechart rather than a set of boolean flags turns illegal transitions into things the machine refuses rather than things a reviewer must notice. The statechart form adds hierarchy and parallel regions to the plain state machine, which is what stops the state explosion that makes flat machines unusable on real lifecycles. The declarative machine definition is also directly inspectable and visualisable, which is a genuine review benefit over transition logic scattered across handlers.
records.applicability_limits: JavaScript and TypeScript only; the equivalent decision in other languages is a different library or a hand-rolled transition table. Modelling everything as a machine is its own over-modelling failure: the pattern earns its keep only where there is a real lifecycle with forbidden transitions. Popularity is not evidence of defect reduction and none is offered.

records.source: David Harel, Statecharts: a visual formalism for complex systems
records.study_design: Formalism proposal with worked examples, not an empirical study
records.version_or_commit: Science of Computer Programming, volume 8, issue 3, June 1987, pages 231-274
records.licence: Elsevier publisher copyright, all rights reserved
records.finding: Plain state diagrams do not scale because states multiply combinatorially. The formalism adds exactly three things to fix that: hierarchy (states that contain states, so a transition can leave a whole cluster at once), orthogonality (concurrent regions, so independent dimensions of state do not multiply), and broadcast communication between regions. This is the origin of every statechart tool in use today and it is why hierarchical state is the right answer to a lifecycle with cross-cutting conditions rather than a flag per condition.
records.applicability_limits: Read at abstract and secondary-description level only; the full text is behind an Elsevier paywall and was not inspected at this access, so no detailed claim about its semantics should be made on this record alone. It is a formalism paper aimed at reactive and real-time systems, not business rules, and it offers no evidence about maintainability or defect rates in business software.
records.review: on-change-of:access to the full text for verification

records.source: RFC 9557, Internet Extended Date/Time Format (IXDTF)
records.licence: IETF Trust Legal Provisions (BSD-style code licence, document reproduction permitted with the required notices)
records.finding: A UTC offset is not a time zone, and storing only the offset loses information the domain needs. An offset is a single number; a zone identifier such as Europe/London is a function from instants to offsets, which is what you need to answer what one day later means across a daylight-saving boundary. The standard therefore extends RFC 3339 with a bracketed zone identifier from the IANA database, plus a calendar tag, and marks each suffix as critical or elective so a reader knows which it must understand. It also reinterprets a trailing Z as UTC is known but local offset is not, which is a distinct fact from the timestamp being in UTC.
records.applicability_limits: Explicitly does not cover future local times whose offset can be changed by a political decision, floating times with no UTC anchor, or non-UTC timescales. It standardises serialisation, not storage or arithmetic, and it is only as good as the tz database revision each system carries.

records.source: TC39 Temporal proposal documentation
records.version_or_commit: proposal documentation as published at tc39.es, inspected 2026-08-03; stage not stated on the page and not verified at this access
records.licence: unknown (no licence statement on the documentation page; the proposal repository states its own terms)
records.finding: Temporal quantities are not one type, they are at least seven, and conflating them is where date bugs come from. An exact instant, a zoned date-time, a calendar date with no time, a wall-clock time with no date, a date-time with no zone, a year-month, a month-day and a duration are all different things with different valid operations. The design rationale is explicit and transferable to any language: separate types stop code silently assuming zero, UTC or the local zone for a value that is genuinely unknown. The domain rule that follows is to choose the narrowest type that holds the fact, so a birthday is a plain date and never a timestamp.
records.applicability_limits: A JavaScript proposal; the type taxonomy transfers as a modelling idea but the API does not. The page did not state the proposal stage at this access, so no claim about standardisation status should rest on this record. Runtime and polyfill availability was not checked.
records.review: on-change-of:Temporal reaching Stage 4 or shipping across major runtimes

records.source: ISO 4217 currency code lists, published by SIX as maintenance agency
records.version_or_commit: code lists as published by SIX at 2026-08-03; most recent amendment effective 2026-01-01, moving BGN to the historical list on Bulgaria's adoption of the euro
records.licence: unknown (lists published free of charge by the maintenance agency; the ISO 4217 standard text itself is sold by ISO and no reuse licence for the lists is stated on the page)
records.finding: Currency is not a string and the number of decimal places is not two. The authoritative lists carry an alphabetic code, a numeric code and a minor unit exponent per currency, and that exponent varies, so the only safe representation of an amount is an integer count of minor units paired with its currency code, never a float and never a bare number. Currencies also retire: the lists are versioned and a currency can move to the historical list, which means a stored amount must keep the code it was denominated in rather than being reinterpreted later.
records.applicability_limits: The lists give codes and exponents, not rounding rules, not allocation rules for splitting an amount without losing pennies, and not conversion. Terms of use for redistributing the lists were not established at this access, so do not vendor the data without checking. The exponent is not always what a payment processor will accept, as EV-0284 shows.
records.review: on-change-of:an ISO 4217 amendment affecting a currency in use

records.source: Stripe documentation, supported currencies and amount representation
records.licence: unknown (Stripe documentation copyright, no open licence stated)
records.finding: The largest payment processor represents every amount as an integer in the currency's minor unit, which is the strongest available confirmation that the integer-minor-unit rule is production practice rather than purism. More useful is what the exceptions teach: ISK and UGX are zero-decimal by the standard but must be sent as hundreds for backwards compatibility, and HUF and TWD are charged with two decimals but paid out only in whole units. The lesson for modelling is that the minor-unit exponent is a property of a currency in a context, so the conversion between domain money and an external system's money belongs in one adapter and nowhere else.
records.applicability_limits: One vendor's API contract, not a standard, and it changes without notice. The quirks listed are specific to Stripe's history and must not be generalised to other processors or to accounting systems. Says nothing about rounding policy, allocation or multi-currency accounting.
records.counter_evidence: The divergence from ISO 4217 in EV-0283 is itself the counter-evidence to treating any single currency table as authoritative across a whole system.

records.source: Alexis King, Parse, don't validate
records.licence: unknown (no licence statement on the post)
records.finding: A validation function throws away what it learned; a parsing function returns a value whose type carries the proof, so no downstream code has to re-check and no downstream code can forget. The operational rules are: narrow the representation at the system boundary and as early as possible, prefer a type that cannot express the illegal state over a check that rejects it, and treat repeated checks of the same fact as the symptom, since scattered validation is what lets inconsistent state through. This is the cheapest form of invariant enforcement because it costs nothing at runtime and cannot be skipped.
records.applicability_limits: The author frames these as ideals rather than requirements and concedes some invariants are genuinely hard to express in a type system. The argument is strongest in languages with sum types and opaque constructors and weakest where the type system cannot restrict construction; in a dynamic language the equivalent is a constructor-enforced value object, not a type. It also does not address invariants that span several objects, which is where aggregates in EV-0269 take over.

records.source: Ozkan, Babur and van den Brand, Domain-Driven Design in software development: a systematic literature review on implementation, challenges, and effectiveness
records.study_design: Systematic literature review with quantitative and qualitative synthesis
records.population: 36 peer-reviewed primary studies on DDD implementation and outcomes
records.version_or_commit: arXiv v4, 2025-06-27; published version in Journal of Systems and Software, 2025
records.licence: arXiv non-exclusive distribution licence v1.0 for the preprint; publisher copyright on the journal version
records.finding: This is the strongest evidence available on whether DDD works, and its most important result is how thin that evidence is. Across 36 peer-reviewed studies the review reports that DDD improved the systems studied and that its main demonstrated use is decomposing systems into services, while also reporting that a number of the primary studies carried no empirical evaluation at all, and that onboarding cost and the need for scarce expertise are recurring reported challenges. The honest reading is that DDD's decomposition value has some support and its correctness or maintainability value largely does not.
records.applicability_limits: A review inherits the weakness of its primaries: mostly case studies and experience reports, with publication bias towards successful adoptions since failed DDD projects rarely produce papers. No effect sizes, no comparison against a competent non-DDD baseline, and the abstract does not name the databases searched. Says nothing about DDD in agent-written codebases.
records.counter_evidence: The review's own finding that onboarding cost and expertise scarcity recur is direct evidence against making heavyweight tactical DDD a default, and supports treating it as a tool selected for a reason.
records.review: on-change-of:a controlled study comparing DDD and non-DDD outcomes on matched systems

records.source: Andreas Hinterhuber, Customer value-based pricing strategies: why companies resist
records.study_design: Two-stage empirical study: qualitative exploration with executives in pricing workshops, then a questionnaire tested on a larger sample
records.population: 81 executives across B2B and B2C industries in Germany, Austria, China and the USA
records.version_or_commit: Journal of Business Strategy 29(4), 2008, article page 41, DOI 10.1108/02756660810887079
records.licence: unknown (Emerald publisher copyright; abstract and secondary summaries consulted, paraphrase only)
records.finding: Value-based pricing is the approach practitioners and academics say works, yet more than eighty per cent of firms still price mainly from cost or from competitor levels. The reported blockers are all capability blockers rather than belief blockers: no method for assessing value, no way to communicate it, no working segmentation, sales incentives that reward volume, and no senior sponsorship. The decision rule that follows is that adopting value-based pricing is an operational build, not a slogan, and the first artefact needed is a value assessment the seller can actually run.
records.applicability_limits: Executive self-report from 2008, pre-SaaS-mainstream, mid-size and large firms, no software or usage-metered products isolated. Says nothing about how a one-person or two-person venture with no sales force should assess value. The eighty per cent figure is a survey-era snapshot and should not be quoted as current.
records.counter_evidence: Later work (EV-0288) finds that competition-informed and cost-informed pricing are not uniformly inferior; their performance depends on conditions such as product advantage and market maturity.
records.review: on-change-of:a newer large-sample replication of pricing-practice prevalence

records.source: Paul T. M. Ingenbleek, Ruud T. Frambach and Tammo H. A. Bijmolt, Best Practices for New Product Pricing: Impact on Market Performance and Price Level under Different Conditions
records.study_design: Cross-sectional management survey of new-product pricing practice, testing value-informed, competition-informed and cost-informed price setting against market performance under moderating conditions
records.population: Survey of production and service companies (a related paper in the same programme reports 144 firms); abstract-level access only
records.version_or_commit: Journal of Product Innovation Management, 2013, DOI 10.1111/jpim.12008
records.licence: unknown (Wiley publisher copyright; full text paywalled at HTTP 402, abstract and indexing records consulted)
records.finding: The three price-setting practices are not a ranking. Value-informed, competition-informed and cost-informed pricing each pay off under different conditions, so the useful question is which information the price should be anchored to given product advantage, competitive intensity and how well the buyer can judge value. A venture should therefore name the practice it is using and the condition that justifies it, rather than declaring one practice correct.
records.applicability_limits: Self-reported survey data, no causal identification, physical and service products rather than metered software. Full text was not obtained, so the specific moderator coefficients are not recorded here and must not be quoted.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0287 frames cost and competitor pricing as a failure of capability; this source frames them as conditionally rational.
records.review: on-change-of:obtaining full text or a newer meta-analysis of pricing practice and performance

records.source: Klaus M. Miller, Reto Hofstetter, Harley Krohmer and Z. John Zhang, How Should Consumers' Willingness to Pay Be Measured? An Empirical Comparison of State-of-the-Art Approaches
records.study_design: Comparison of four willingness-to-pay elicitation methods (open-ended question, choice-based conjoint, Becker-DeGroot-Marschak mechanism, incentive-aligned choice-based conjoint) against real purchase data
records.population: Consumer respondents with a real purchase benchmark condition
records.benchmark: Real purchase behaviour as the criterion
records.version_or_commit: Journal of Marketing Research 48(1), 2011, pages 172-184, DOI 10.1509/jmkr.48.1.172
records.licence: unknown (SAGE and American Marketing Association copyright; abstract consulted, paraphrase only)
records.finding: Only the incentive-compatible methods (BDM and incentive-aligned conjoint) passed both statistical and decision-oriented tests against real purchases. Hypothetical elicitation overstates willingness to pay; respondents are measurably more price sensitive when their answer costs them something. The decision rule is that a stated price a customer never had to honour is weak evidence, and any price derived from a survey should be treated as an upper bound until a real transaction tests it.
records.applicability_limits: Consumer product context with a single purchase occasion. Does not cover B2B committee buying, multi-year contracts, or metered products where willingness to pay is a function of realised usage. Incentive-compatible methods are hard to run for a service that does not yet exist.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0290 reports work claiming the hypothetical Van Westendorp meter can nonetheless reach predictive quality comparable to BDM, which cuts against a blanket dismissal of hypothetical methods.
records.review: on-change-of:a replication comparing hypothetical and incentive-aligned WTP for subscription software

records.source: Sawtooth Software, Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter explainer
records.finding: The four-question price sensitivity meter yields an acceptable range from crossing cumulative curves, and the vendor that sells pricing research states its own limits plainly: it has no competitive context, the curve crossing does not follow from economic theory, and it predicts no purchase volume. Useful as a cheap first bracket on a price range, never as the price decision itself.
records.applicability_limits: A screening instrument only. Results move with the sample frame and with how the product is described, and the method assumes the respondent can imagine the product accurately. Not usable for tier design or for metered pricing.
records.counter_evidence: Published evaluations report the meter is biased by its hypothetical framing and its focus on minimum customer resistance, while also reporting predictive quality comparable to incentive-aligned BDM in at least one comparison; the literature has not settled this.

records.source: Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester, Effects of $9 Price Endings on Retail Sales: Evidence from Field Experiments
records.study_design: Three randomised field experiments with a catalogue retailer, manipulating price endings on live merchandise
records.population: Retail catalogue customers
records.version_or_commit: Quantitative Marketing and Economics 1(1), March 2003, pages 93-110, DOI 10.1023/A:1023581927405
records.licence: unknown (Springer publisher copyright; abstract and author-hosted copy at Kellogg consulted)
records.finding: A price ending in nine raised demand in all three field experiments, and raised it more for items new to the customer than for items sold in previous years. The effect weakened when sale cues were present. The transferable principle is that price endings are an information cue that works when the buyer has little else to judge by, so the cue is worth most at launch and decays as the buyer learns the category.
records.applicability_limits: US catalogue retail of physical goods in the late 1990s. No evidence offered for B2B, for subscription list prices, or for prices that appear beside a competitor comparison table. Effect sizes are context-specific and should not be transplanted as a rule of thumb.
records.counter_evidence: The same paper notes nine-endings are less effective with sale cues, which is why retailers do not use them everywhere; a blanket charm-pricing rule is not supported.
records.review: on-change-of:a field replication of price-ending effects in subscription software

records.source: Daniel Kahneman, Jack L. Knetsch and Richard Thaler, Fairness as a Constraint on Profit Seeking: Entitlements in the Market
records.study_design: Telephone survey experiments presenting respondents with hypothetical firm actions and eliciting fairness judgements
records.population: General public respondents in Canadian and US cities
records.licence: unknown (American Economic Association copyright; author-hosted copies at Chicago Booth and MIT consulted, paraphrase only)
records.finding: Dual entitlement: buyers accept a price rise that protects the seller's existing margin against a cost increase, and judge a rise that merely exploits a demand shift or scarcity to be unfair. The operational rule is that a price change should be announced with its cause, and that cause should be a cost or a delivered-value change rather than an observed willingness to pay, because the perceived reason drives the retention consequence rather than the number itself.
records.applicability_limits: Stated fairness judgements from 1986 telephone surveys, not observed churn. Fairness norms vary by market, and buyers of a product they depend on may behave differently from survey respondents. The paper does not quantify how much revenue a fairness violation costs.
records.counter_evidence: Firms routinely raise prices on demand shifts without visible collapse, so fairness is a constraint with an unmeasured price rather than a hard prohibition.
records.review: on-change-of:a modern field study linking price-rise framing to measured churn

records.source: Sybil Yang and Michael Lynn, More Evidence Challenging the Robustness and Usefulness of the Attraction Effect
records.study_design: Large set of replication attempts of the asymmetric dominance (decoy) effect using realistic product descriptions and images
records.population: Ninety-one attempts covering 23 product classes and 73 decoyed choice sets
records.version_or_commit: Journal of Marketing Research 51(4), 2014, pages 508-513, DOI 10.1509/jmr.14.0020
records.licence: unknown (SAGE and American Marketing Association copyright; abstract consulted, paraphrase only)
records.finding: Only 11 of 91 attempts produced a reliable attraction effect once stimuli were realistic rather than abstract two-attribute numbers. The decoy tier is therefore not a reliable lever: a pricing page built on the assumption that a deliberately worse middle option will steer buyers is building on an effect that mostly fails to appear outside stylised laboratory setups.
records.applicability_limits: Consumer choice tasks, not live pricing pages with real money and real switching costs. Absence of a reliable effect in these replications does not prove the effect is never present in a specific product; it removes the licence to assume it.
records.counter_evidence: Defenders argue the effect holds when the original conditions are replicated closely, and later experimental work reports asymmetric dominance effects when choices carry economic consequences. The literature is contested, not closed.
records.review: on-change-of:a pre-registered field test of decoy tiers on live pricing pages

records.source: Hema Yoganarasimhan, Ebrahim Barzegary and Abhishek Pani, Design and Evaluation of Optimal Free Trials
records.study_design: Large-scale randomised field experiment assigning new users to 7, 14 or 30 day free trials, plus policy evaluation of personalised trial assignment
records.population: New users of a leading SaaS firm
records.version_or_commit: Management Science 69(6), 2023, pages 3220-3240, DOI 10.1287/mnsc.2022.4507; author copy at faculty.washington.edu
records.licence: unknown (INFORMS copyright on the published version; author-hosted working copy consulted)
records.finding: Shorter trials won. A uniform 7 day trial was the best single policy, raising subscriptions by about 5.6 per cent against the incumbent longer trial. The mechanism was consumer learning rather than demand cannibalisation, and long stretches of inactivity at the end of a trial predicted non-conversion. Experienced users benefited from longer trials, beginners from shorter. The rule: trial length is a variable to test, the default should be short, and time-to-first-value is the thing being bought.
records.applicability_limits: One SaaS firm, one product category, self-serve consumer-like funnel. Says nothing about B2B pilots with procurement, or about products whose value only appears after a full billing cycle of data. The 5.6 per cent figure is firm-specific.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0295 reports a longer trial beating a shorter one on the same outcome family in a different product; the two together suggest an interior optimum rather than a monotone rule.

records.source: Longer or shorter? A large-scale randomized field experiment on the impact of free trial duration on sustainable user conversion in the Freemium model
records.study_design: Randomised field experiment comparing a 3 day control trial with a 7 day treatment trial, analysed through a three-stage conversion model (trial adoption, immediate conversion, delayed conversion)
records.population: 680,588 new users across 190 countries of a global image-editing SaaS provider; enrolled 18 July to 8 August 2022, observed to 15 July 2024
records.benchmark: Trial adoption, immediate conversion, delayed conversion, overall subscription rate
records.licence: CC BY (Creative Commons Attribution, as stated on the article page)
records.finding: Extending the trial from 3 to 7 days raised trial adoption by about 11 per cent and delayed conversion by about 42 per cent, with no significant effect on immediate conversion, and overall subscriptions up about 21 per cent. Conversion is a funnel with distinct stages, and a change can move the late stage while leaving the early stage flat, so a trial-length test judged only on immediate conversion will read as a null and be abandoned wrongly.
records.applicability_limits: The authors state the study covers short-duration trials for utility-based SaaS and that external generalisability remains to be validated. Single firm, consumer-facing creative tool, and the comparison is 3 versus 7 days, not 7 versus 30.
records.counter_evidence: EV-0294 finds 7 days beats 14 and 30 in a different SaaS firm. Read together, the evidence supports roughly a week rather than a monotone longer-is-better or shorter-is-better rule.
records.review: on-change-of:a replication outside creative consumer SaaS

records.source: Peter S. Fader and Bruce G. S. Hardie, How to Project Customer Retention
records.study_design: Probability model derivation and empirical validation: shifted beta-geometric model fitted to observed contractual cohort retention and used to forecast held-out periods
records.population: Contractual (subscription) customer cohorts
records.model: Shifted beta-geometric (sBG), heterogeneity in churn probability modelled as a beta distribution
records.version_or_commit: Journal of Interactive Marketing 21(1), 2007, DOI 10.1002/dir.20074; revisited in a later paper hosted at brucehardie.com
records.licence: unknown (publisher copyright; author-hosted copies at Wharton and brucehardie.com consulted, paraphrase only)
records.finding: Observed cohort retention rates rise over time even when no individual customer changes behaviour, because the high-churn customers leave first and the survivors are a progressively better-retaining mix. A single average churn rate applied forward is therefore the wrong projection, and lifetime value computed as revenue divided by a blended churn rate is systematically wrong. Fit heterogeneity, project by cohort, and report retention as a curve rather than a number.
records.applicability_limits: Contractual settings with clean renew-or-lapse events; non-contractual and usage-metered revenue need different models. Needs several periods of cohort data before it can be fitted, which a venture in its first year does not have. The model says nothing about why customers churn or what price change would alter it.
records.review: on-change-of:adoption of a different CLV model family in the pack

records.source: IFRS 15 Revenue from Contracts with Customers, IFRS Foundation
records.version_or_commit: IFRS 15 as issued, effective for annual reporting periods beginning on or after 1 January 2018; standard page as at 2026
records.licence: unknown (IFRS Foundation copyright, trade marks asserted, no open licence stated on the page; paraphrase only)
records.finding: Revenue follows a five-step model: identify the contract, identify distinct performance obligations, determine the transaction price including variable consideration, allocate that price across obligations by relative stand-alone selling price, and recognise as control transfers. The consequence for packaging is direct: every bundle, discount and add-on has to be decomposable into obligations with defensible stand-alone selling prices, so a tier structure invented purely for the pricing page creates an accounting problem later. Cash collected is not revenue earned.
records.applicability_limits: IFRS applies where the entity reports under IFRS; a UK micro-entity may report under FRS 102 or FRS 105 with different detail, and US filers apply ASC 606. Nothing here sets a price; it constrains how a chosen structure is recognised and reported.
records.review: on-change-of:amendments to IFRS 15 or a change in the venture's reporting framework

records.source: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, Part 4 Chapter 2 (subscription contracts)
records.version_or_commit: 2024 c. 13, Part 4 Chapter 2 as enacted; most provisions not in force at Royal Assent per section 339(1); commencement regulations awaited
records.finding: The subscription regime turns pricing mechanics into statutory duties: key pre-contract information given separately and in writing (s256), an express acknowledgement of the payment obligation at the final online step (s257), reminder notices before renewal payments at six-monthly intervals (s258, s259), a straightforward online exit route (s260), acknowledgement and refund of overpayments (s261), and unconditional 14 day cooling-off both initially and after specified renewals (s264, s265, s266). Designing a renewal flow that assumes silence equals consent is designing against the direction of law.
records.applicability_limits: Consumer subscription contracts in the UK only; B2B subscriptions are out of scope, as are services paid for only with data. Commercial commentary at the access date reported the regime pushed back to spring 2027, so the duties are not yet live and the detail may change in the implementing regulations.
records.counter_evidence: Repeated commencement delays mean building to the full regime today is a bet on final wording that has not been made; the cheap position is to satisfy the principles without hard-coding the section detail.
records.review: on-change-of:commencement regulations for DMCC Part 4 Chapter 2

records.source: Competition and Markets Authority, Unfair commercial practices guidance (CMA207)
records.version_or_commit: CMA207, first published 4 April 2025, updated 18 November 2025 to reflect the separate price transparency guidance CMA209
records.finding: Since the consumer provisions of the DMCC Act commenced in April 2025 the CMA enforces consumer law directly, with fines reported up to ten per cent of global turnover, and drip pricing is expressly banned: unavoidable mandatory charges must appear in the headline price rather than at the end of the journey. The binding rule for any pricing page is that the advertised price includes everything the buyer cannot avoid paying.
records.applicability_limits: UK business-to-consumer trading. Guidance is the regulator's view, not the statute, and the detail sits in the Act and in CMA209. Optional extras and genuinely variable charges are treated differently from unavoidable ones, and that boundary is where disputes will sit.

records.source: Competition and Markets Authority, Evidence review of online choice architecture and consumer and competition harm
records.study_design: Regulator literature review synthesising academic and empirical evidence on 21 online choice architecture practices
records.version_or_commit: Evidence review paper dated 14 April 2022, companion to the CMA discussion paper on online choice architecture
records.finding: The review classifies 21 practices into choice structure, choice information and choice pressure, and identifies a subset (drip pricing, sludge, dark nudges, decoys and choice overload, sensory manipulation, information overload) that the literature finds almost always harmful. This gives a design test with a regulator's own words behind it: if a pricing or checkout pattern appears on that list, it is a liability rather than a growth tactic, whatever it does to short-term conversion.
records.applicability_limits: A synthesis, not new primary research, and the underlying studies vary in quality; the 2022 vintage predates the DMCC enforcement regime. It labels practices as harmful without quantifying harm per practice for a specific business.
records.counter_evidence: The same body of literature contains contested effects; the decoy evidence in EV-0293 shows one of the listed practices often fails to work at all, so harm and efficacy are separate questions.

records.source: GOV.UK, Late commercial payments: charging interest and debt recovery
records.version_or_commit: Guidance page as accessed 2026-08-03 (no update date shown on the page)
records.finding: Where no payment term is agreed, a commercial payment is late 30 days after the later of invoice receipt and delivery. Agreed terms may run to 60 days between businesses, or longer only if fair to both, and must be within 30 days for public authorities. So a quoted price without a stated payment term still has a term, set by statute, and the contract's job is to make it explicit rather than to invent it.
records.applicability_limits: UK commercial (business to business and public sector) transactions. Statutory interest rate and fixed debt recovery amounts sit on linked pages that were not fetched, so those figures are not recorded here. Consumer contracts are governed separately.

records.source: Procurement Act 2023, section 68 (implied payment terms in public contracts)
records.version_or_commit: 2023 c. 54, section 68; in force 24 February 2025, not in force at Royal Assent
records.finding: Every public contract carries an implied term that sums due are paid within 30 days of a valid invoice, or the later due date on the invoice, and any term purporting to restrict or override that is without effect. A valid invoice needs the supplier name, a description of what was supplied, the amount and a unique identifier. Selling to the public sector therefore imports a payment clock the buyer cannot negotiate away, and the seller's own invoicing discipline is what starts it.
records.applicability_limits: UK public contracts under the Procurement Act regime that went live on 24 February 2025; devolved and transitional arrangements vary, and contracts procured under the old regulations continue under those. Section 73 flows the term down to sub-contracts. Does not apply to private-sector customers.
records.review: on-change-of:Procurement Act commencement or amendment affecting Part 4

records.source: GOV.UK, VAT registration: when to register
records.version_or_commit: Guidance page as accessed 2026-08-03, stating the 90,000 pound threshold (no update date shown on the page)
records.finding: Registration is compulsory once taxable turnover over any rolling 12 months exceeds 90,000 pounds, or is expected to exceed it within the next 30 days, with registration due within 30 days of the month end and an effective date on the first day of the second following month. For a small venture this is a pricing event, not just an admin event: crossing it changes the effective price to consumer buyers by the VAT rate unless the headline price is restructured in advance.
records.applicability_limits: UK VAT only, and the threshold is a policy number that changes at fiscal events. The deregistration threshold and the treatment of digital services supplied cross-border are not covered by this page and must be checked separately.
records.review: on-change-of:UK Budget alteration of the VAT registration threshold

records.source: GOV.UK, Find out if and when you need to use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax
records.finding: Sole traders and landlords in Self Assessment must use Making Tax Digital for Income Tax from 6 April 2026 where qualifying income exceeded 50,000 pounds in 2024-25, from 6 April 2027 above 30,000 pounds, and from 6 April 2028 above 20,000 pounds. The control implication is that the venture's books must be digital and quarterly-reportable from the start, so the finance stack is a founding decision rather than a year-two clean-up.
records.applicability_limits: UK unincorporated businesses and landlords; companies file corporation tax separately and are not in scope of this timetable. The page gives thresholds and dates only, not the record-keeping or quarterly update mechanics, which sit in linked guidance not fetched here. Thresholds and dates have moved before.
records.review: on-change-of:HMRC alteration of the MTD for Income Tax timetable

records.source: Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS), Bitol, LF AI and Data Foundation
records.version_or_commit: v3.1.0; 607 commits on main; media type application/odcs+yaml;version=3.1.0
records.finding: A data contract is a single machine-readable document covering schema, quality rules, service levels, owning team and support channel together. Splitting those into separate artefacts is what lets a table keep its schema while quietly losing its freshness guarantee, because nobody owns the gap between them.
records.applicability_limits: A document format, not an enforcement engine: nothing in the standard runs the quality rules or measures the service level, and adoption outside the Bitol tool circle is still small. The pricing and infrastructure sections are aimed at inter-company data sharing and are dead weight inside a single venture.
records.counter_evidence: Competing formats exist (the Open Data Product Specification, vendor-native contract schemas in dbt), so committing to ODCS is a bet on a format war that is not settled.

records.source: Schelter, Lange, Schmidt, Celikel, Biessmann and Grafberger, Automating Large-Scale Data Quality Verification (Deequ)
records.study_design: System description with experimental evaluation on several datasets at Amazon
records.population: Production data pipelines at a large online retailer
records.benchmark: Internal datasets; incremental metric computation and anomaly detection experiments
records.licence: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (stated on the paper); paraphrase only, no reuse of wording
records.finding: Data quality checks are declarative constraints compiled into aggregation queries, so the check runs as part of the pipeline rather than as a separate audit. Two mechanisms matter beyond assertions: incremental computation of metrics over growing datasets, so the cost does not scale with history, and anomaly detection over the time series of past metric values, which catches drift that no fixed threshold was written for.
records.applicability_limits: Built for Spark-scale batch data at a retailer; the incremental machinery is unnecessary below a few million rows, where a full rescan is cheaper than the state it saves. Constraint suggestion learns from the data as it is, so it will happily suggest a rule that encodes a current bug as the norm.
records.counter_evidence: The paper's own framing (unit tests for data) presumes the producer knows the invariants. The anomaly-detection path exists precisely because that presumption fails, which is an admission that declared-rule approaches such as dbt contracts do not cover the failure that actually bites.

records.source: dbt Labs, How we structure our dbt projects
records.licence: unknown (no licence statement on the page)
records.finding: Layer transformations by how far they have travelled from the source, not by subject: staging models are one-to-one with source tables and do only cleaning and renaming, intermediate models hold the joins and logic, and marts are wide business entities. The value is that a naming prefix tells you what a model is allowed to do, so review is mechanical.
records.applicability_limits: Vendor guidance for one transformation tool, presented as convention with no measurement behind it. The three-layer split adds model count and build time, which is real cost on a small warehouse. It says nothing about dimensional design inside the marts layer.
records.counter_evidence: The recommendation to land on wide business entities sits against Kimball dimensional practice, which keeps facts narrow and joins to conformed dimensions. Both are widely used and the guide does not argue the difference.

records.source: Kimball Group, Dimensional Modeling Techniques
records.version_or_commit: page as served 2026-08-03; underlying technique PDF dated 2013-09
records.licence: All rights reserved, The Kimball Group; paraphrase only
records.finding: Three decisions carry dimensional modelling and they are made in order: declare the grain of the fact table first, then the dimensions that apply at that grain, then the facts. Conformed dimensions are the integration mechanism, letting separate fact tables be compared without a central model. The slowly changing dimension types are a numbered menu of history policies (overwrite, new row, new column and hybrids), which turns an argument about history into a choice from a list.
records.applicability_limits: Formalised for on-premises relational warehouses where storage and joins were expensive; the cost argument for surrogate keys and narrow facts is much weaker on columnar cloud storage. The site has not been substantially updated since the Kimball Group wound down, so treat it as a settled body of technique, not a maintained one.
records.counter_evidence: Modern practice frequently lands on wide denormalised marts (see the dbt structure guide) and skips surrogate keys entirely; the grain-first and conformed-dimension arguments survive that shift, the physical prescriptions largely do not.

records.source: Armbrust, Ghodsi, Xin and Zaharia, Lakehouse: A New Generation of Open Platforms that Unify Data Warehousing and Advanced Analytics
records.study_design: Position paper with a TPC-DS performance comparison against cloud data warehouses
records.population: Enterprise analytics platforms
records.licence: unknown (no licence statement on the paper)
records.finding: The failure mode of the two-tier lake-plus-warehouse shape is not performance, it is that the same facts exist twice with an ETL hop between them, producing staleness, reliability gaps and duplicated cost. The argued fix is one copy in an open direct-access format with a metadata layer over it giving transactions and schema enforcement, and the paper reports TPC-DS results competitive with cloud warehouses to show the performance objection is answerable.
records.applicability_limits: Written by the vendor whose product is the lakehouse, so the architectural claim and the commercial interest coincide. TPC-DS is a synthetic decision-support benchmark and does not represent interactive product analytics. The argument presumes machine learning and unstructured data are in scope; for a venture doing SQL over structured events, the second-generation problem it solves may never arise.
records.counter_evidence: Directly contradicted on scale grounds by Tigani's account of BigQuery workloads, where most customers hold under a terabyte and most queries scan under 100 MB, at which point the two-tier problem the lakehouse solves does not exist because there is no lake.

records.source: Apache Iceberg
records.version_or_commit: unknown exact release; main branch at 8,992 commits, inspected 2026-08-03; format specification versioned separately
records.finding: An open table format is the seam that stops a warehouse choice from becoming a data lock-in: the table metadata (snapshots, schema evolution, partition evolution) lives with the files, so Spark, Trino, Flink and others read the same table without an export. Buying a query engine and owning your table format are separable decisions.
records.applicability_limits: Catalogue operation, compaction and snapshot expiry are ongoing maintenance work that a managed warehouse does for you; below a few terabytes that overhead usually exceeds the lock-in it avoids. The format specification and the Java implementation move at different speeds from the Python, Go and Rust implementations, so multi-engine parity is a claim to verify per feature, not a given.

records.source: Jordan Tigani, Big Data is Dead (MotherDuck blog)
records.study_design: Practitioner account of internal BigQuery telemetry; figures recalled, not published
records.population: Google BigQuery customers
records.finding: Storage size and working set are different quantities and only the second sets the architecture. From BigQuery experience the author reports most customers holding under a terabyte in total and around ninety per cent of queries scanning under 100 MB, a power-law distribution in which even large enterprises mostly run small queries. The decision rule that follows: size the analytics stack to the query working set, and treat distributed processing as something to justify, not assume.
